en: [Introduction] 0.1 ... Surely that lion which shatters the truth has been unleashed by me... there is no such fruit as heaven and so forth.
True; however, even by those who know the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the worldly path must be followed for the sake of experiencing the results of actions already undertaken. ...
In regard to worldly convention, the fool and the wise man are alike.
And so forth.
[Objection: But if the principles (*tattva*) are a delusion (*upaplava*), why shall we explain the reality according to the way things truly are (*yathārtha*)?
Earth, water, fire, and air are the principles.
The designation "body," "sense-faculty," and "object" applies to that collection [of atoms], and so forth;
it is not for any other purpose.
For what purpose? For the purpose of producing a reflection.
What, then, is being reflected here?
The principles such as earth and so forth are well-known in the world;
yet even these, when subjected to investigation, do not remain established.
What, then, of the others? Now, how is it that they do not exist?
This is explained: the establishment of pride is based upon the characteristic of existence (*sallakṣaṇa*).
And the status of the object of cognition is dependent upon the means of cognition;
in the absence of that [means], how could those two be the objects of the conventional usage of "existent"?
If, however, such a conventional usage is not performed... [then they would not exist].
Therefore, the conventional usage of the existence of form (*rūpa*) in the self and the conventional usage of the existence of pleasure (*sukha*) in a jar and so forth must be established.

[Chapter 1: Examination of the Nyāya Definition of Perception] 1. "Perception is cognition produced by the contact of a sense faculty with its object, which is non-verbal, non-erroneous, and of a determinate nature"—this is its definition.

1.1 And as for that non-deviation... is it by virtue of being produced by a collection of unimpaired causal factors, or rather by being free from sublation, or by the efficacy of purposeful action, or otherwise?
1.11 If that non-deviation were by virtue of being produced by a collection of unimpaired causal factors, by what means is that very non-defectiveness of the causes apprehended?
It is not by means of direct perception, because the skill of the eyes and so forth is beyond the reach of the senses;
nor is it by means of inference.
Because no other mark (liṅga) is apprehended.
[Objection: But surely this very cognition is the mark; arising from that [object], it makes known its qualified nature.
[Response: If this were so, an unavoidable circularity (itaretarāśrayatva) would result.
Furthermore, if the sense faculties were the locus of defects and excellences, then the suspicion of defect would not be avoided in the cognition arising from them,
just as in the case of verbal cognition produced by human activity (puṃvyāpāra).
Alternatively, if non-erroneousness is known through the non-arising of sublation (bādhā), [then...]

We are in doubt as to whether the non-arising of sublation in a cognition is due to its apprehending an object as it truly is, or rather due to the deficiency of the causal factors that produce a sublating cognition;
for indeed, the non-arising of sublation is observed to result from the deficiency of the causal factors that produce a sublating cognition.
For example, when the cognition of water arises regarding a distant mass of shimmering rays, no sublation occurs.
When one situated in the place of practice encounters the causal factors (*kāraka*), [the result] arises;
and as it is arising, it comes into being through various durations of time such as a year;
yet sometimes, due to the deficiency of causal factors, it does not come to fruition at all.
Nor does its correspondence with reality (yathārthatā) follow from this much alone; moreover, the very absence of sublation (*bādhā*) is what makes known the existence of sublation,
because the existence of that [sublation] is apprehended through the non-apprehension of it.
1.12 Furthermore, regarding the absence of sublation (*bādhāviraha*): is it with respect to all persons, or rather with respect to the cognizer?
If it were with respect to all persons, then even their absence [of sublation] would require omniscience on our part.
Let them all be omniscient; what is the harm in that?
Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the absence of any conventional usage regarding non-omniscience.
Now, if— relative to the cognizer— there is no sublation, meaning that no subverting cognition arises for the cognizer,
then by that [absence], it is non-deviant.
That is incorrect,

because even when no subverting cognition arises for the cognizer, one observes erroneous cognitions regarding a jewel, a mirage, and so forth, due to such causes as traveling to another place or death; or else, that erroneous cognition arises in precisely such a manner by entering into the very nature of its own origin.
That which acts as an obstacle to the arising of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-vijñāna*)—
its destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is likewise of that same nature, just like the "correct knowledge" (*samyag-jñāna*) desired by others.
This being so, what was stated— that "that cognition whose instrument is defective and wherein there is a conviction of falsity is itself an incorrect cognition"— is precisely what is incorrect.
1.13 Now, if you understand non-deviation through the efficacy of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti-sāmarthya*), [then consider this:
the efficacy of purposeful activity is the connection with a result (*phala*);
and the result consists of such things as garlands, sandalwood, women, and water.
Because the fruits of truth are realized within them, there is a metaphorical designation of "fruit" applied to them;
their connection with that body is the capacity for activity. Activity is the movement residing in the body.
That capacity leads to the understanding of non-deviation.
Is that [capacity] already understood or not understood?
If it is not understood, [then...]
How do you know that it exists?
If it has been understood,
then one must follow what was stated previously regarding how the non-deviation of that understanding is itself understood.
1.13 By the attainment of water, the non-erroneous nature of the previously arisen cognition of water is established.
Is this by the attainment of the very water that appeared [in the cognition], or by the attainment of water of the same kind, or by the attainment of water belonging to that lineage?
If it were by the attainment of the water that appeared, [then...]
That is incorrect;
the persistence of water produced by reflection is not tenable,
because its disappearance is possible through the process of motion in its constituent parts arising from the impact of the turning of fish or buffaloes.

1.13a2 Now, if [the validity] were due to obtaining water of that same kind, then in that case, even when a cognition of water has arisen in the absence of actual water, men would obtain water somewhere;
that too would have to be non-erroneous.

If it is argued that false cognition does not bring about water connected with that specific place and time, whereas right cognition does bring about water connected with that specific place and time, and therefore the latter is non-deviant;
That which does not lead to attainment is deviant;
if that were so, then the cognition of one about to die and the perception of the moon, sun, planets, constellations, stars, and so forth would also be deviant.
Nor does it possess the quality of bringing about water connected to that specific place and time, because the place itself, like the water, is subject to destruction.
Furthermore, the existence of a universal (jāti) is not possible.
How is that very [nature] so?
It is explained as being non-different, different, or both different and non-different from the individual instances of water.
(a) If it were established as identical [to them],...
Therefore, in this case, because they are manifold, its [the universal's] manifoldness is established;
and if it were one, the consequence would be that all of them are one.
Furthermore, if there were oneness, there would either be an absence of generality or a contradiction with the nature of identity.
a.2 Now, if that [universal] were a distinct entity, it would either have an excluded form (*vyāvṛttākāra*) or a conforming form (*anugatākāra*). If it has an excluded form,
it cannot possess the nature of a universal, because its intrinsic nature is exclusively excluded, just like water and other such things.
Now, if it is of a continuous nature, is that continuity of its own form or of another's form?
If it were a continuity of its own form, [then...]
That is incorrect,
because there is no persistence within the self; or else, [if it were to exist], it would be permeated by the nature of another.
What is this state of being permeated by another form? Is it identity with that, or inherence in that?
If it were identity, it would entail the consequence of non-difference between the universal and its possessor.
Now, if it is argued that "pervasion" consists in inherence in the form of another, that is incorrect;
for inherence is distinct from the universal.
One begins to examine the inclusive nature of the universal (*sāmānya*),
and not anything other than that.
(A.2a) Furthermore, if the non-erroneousness of the previously mentioned cognition of water is established through the attainment of an object belonging to the class of water, [then...]
In that case, since the genus "water-ness" (*udakajāti*) is also possible in cows and the like,
there would be a non-deviant cognition of water through the apprehension of cows and so forth.
If it is argued that "water-ness" does not exist in cows and the like, [the response follows].
Is it mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), non-existence after destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), or absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*)?
If it were mutual non-existence, then that would apply equally to water and so forth, resulting in the undesirable consequence that the nature of "water-ness" would be absent even in water;
for the form of water is not the same as water-ness, and water-ness is not the same as water.
If it were prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), then there would follow the consequence that even in water, the nature of water (*udakatva*) does not exist.
If it were posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), then there would likewise follow the consequence that it does not exist even in water.
If, on the other hand, it exists elsewhere...
It is not possible for that which has ceased in one place to arise elsewhere.
If, on the other hand, it were an absolute non-existence, then it would follow that water also lacks that [nature of being water].
If you argue that water lacks the nature of being water in cows and the like because of the absence of a relation [between them], then...

In that case as well, one must state— as before— whether it is mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), or absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
If it is argued that [the absence of "water-ness" in cows and the like] is due to the absence of other causes,
that [reasoning] applies equally here as well.
Furthermore, it is not possible to establish a plurality among individual instances of water.
Water is distinguished from the form of non-water by its having the form of water; but how is it distinguished from the form of water itself?
Is it by way of having the form of water, or rather by way of another form?
If it is excluded by way of having the form of water, then other instances of water would consequently lack the form of water, just as [other things lack] taste and so forth.
If it were to cease its appearance as water by virtue of having the form of non-water, then it would follow that it is not water, just like fire and other such things.
If it is argued that even though there is the specific nature of the form of water, there is nevertheless an imagined distinction of internal sub-varieties (gaṇikākāra), [we reply:]...
It is true that the form of the intermediate wave is established either as identical to or as non-identical with the water.
If it were established as identical,
then by virtue of having the form of water, it would be indistinguishable from other water.
In this way, it follows that other individual instances of water would lack the nature of water;
the refutation has already been stated previously.
Now, suppose it is established as not being of that same nature (*atādātmya*).
In that case, it would be like [the absence of] "non-water-ness" in taste and so forth.
Or, by the exclusion of "water-ness," it would be excluded from the form of "non-water.
Let these wise ones listen to this prattle of a child!
If water is excluded from non-water by the exclusion of "water-ness," then how is "water-ness" itself excluded from both water and non-water?
There exists no other universal (*jāti*) that could serve as its differentiator.
Or, if it were accepted [that they do not differ], there would follow the consequence of undesirable calamities.
Therefore, they are distinguished from one another by their own specific forms,
not by means of a universal (*jāti*) or other such categories.
Because it would follow that there is no exclusion of [the properties of] genus and so forth.
Therefore, it is established that the plurality of individual water-entities is not tenable;
since that is untenable, there exists no universal called "water-ness," just as there is none for "ownership."
For this reason as well, a universal does not exist, because that which is permanent cannot logically be a producer of cognition.

How so? It is explained: the very same nature—which is of the essence of a universal, possesses power, and exists in the form of a capacity—independent of other causal factors during the state of producing cognition, is that very same nature during the state of non-production.
Therefore, it would follow that the effect must have been produced even previously;
or, if it were not produced then, it would not produce it now either.
Alternatively, if it produces the effect by depending on another causal factor, [then that other factor must also depend on yet another].
What is done for that [permanent entity] by another factor (kāraka)—is its status as a factor produced, or is it made known?
If it is produced, then its permanence is well-established;
if it is made known, then its status as a factor is already established.

Even in the absence of that [cause], because it illuminates what already exists, let it be a causal factor; what is the fault? The undesirable consequence would be the production of an effect [even without a cause].
Furthermore, even if it were a causal factor (*kāraka*), if it did not produce an effect— oh, how weighty is the royal decree of the Naiyāyika-beast!
For this reason as well, there is no such thing as a universal (*sāmānya*), because there is no means of valid cognition (*māna*) to establish it.
Is there not indeed a means of valid cognition for the similarity between these two, their correspondence,
such that "this is similar to that"?

The cognition that "this is indeed similar to that," and so forth, which makes known the existence of a universal, is not possible for one who has not yet apprehended the universal; yet this cognition exists, being free from sublation and establishing the subtle nature of the genus. This [position] is untenable.
Is such knowledge produced by that [object] acting as a cause (*nimitta*), or by it having become an object of action (*karmatāpanna*)? If it is produced by it acting as a cause,
then a universal (*sāmānya*) need not be postulated.
The cause is indeed of an uncommon nature; it is sufficient for the production of such a cognition of a universal that one need not postulate a [real] universal.
If, on the other hand, it were produced by something that has become an object, then that [universal] would be non-existent.
A universal does not appear at all in consciousness for those whose awareness has not been subverted by deceivers.
[Objection: But surely a resemblance appears. [Reply: True, it appears.
It is not denied; rather, while existing as consisting of substance, quality, and action, just as there is "cook-ness" among the various distinctions such as cooks,
[so too are they] these cooks.
This should also be understood in the case of specific attributes (viśeṣa) and so forth, such as "this one is similar to that cook" or "that one is similar to this.
If it is argued that even here there is a cognition of a universal (sāmānya), [we reply:]...
It is not so, because it would contradict the Sūtras; for since there is no further generality or particularity within generalities and particulars, cognition arises from those alone.

Furthermore, if one were to postulate a generality within the particulars, there would be an infinite regress, and when such doubt exists, another particularity would have to be postulated among them.
Furthermore, since the universal would thus be infinite [in its regress], enough with this adherence to a false obsession. Now,
if you propose that the universal is both different and non-different from the individuals— being perceived as distinct from the individuals due to a difference in form (*ākāra*),
yet being non-distinct because it is not perceived as having a difference in location (*deśa*)— then it is a separate entity.
This is a great well-spoken statement:
things do not differ merely by difference of location; rather, entities attain distinction solely through difference of form.
And how there is no difference in form has just been explained immediately above.
(b) It is not the case that a universal exists in individuals by way of inherence (*samavāya*), for such [inherence] does not exist.
(b.1) For inherence must have either an exclusive nature or a pervasive nature.
If it has a nature that is exclusively excluded [from others],
to what would this inherence belong, given its exclusion from everything, like blue and so forth? Or, if it has a nature that is inclusive [of all things]—
In that case, it is a universal (sāmānya), not inherence (samavāya),
because it exists eternally and resides in multiple locations, like "cowness" (gotva) and so forth.
b.2 And because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes it.
b.21 [Objection: "But surely this is determined by perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣabuddhi*).
[Reply: That is incorrect.
Is it determined by the cognition of a relation, or is it expressed by the cognition of "here-ness" (ihabuddhi) or the cognition of inherence (samavāyabuddhi)?
If it is by the cognition of a relation, what is this relation?

Is the relation (sambandha) that which is endowed with a genus of relation, or is it produced from multiple substrata, or does it reside in multiple things, or is it a specific cognition of relation, or is it that which produces the cognition of relation, or is it the form of the cognition of relation? If, for you, the relation is that which is endowed with a genus of relation, that is untenable.
Otherwise, there would be the consequence that inherence (samavāya) lacks the nature of a relation.
If, on the other hand, it is produced from multiple material causes, then there would be the consequence that even a jar or similar objects would possess the nature of a relation.

If, on the other hand, the relation is that which resides in multiple [entities], then it would follow that the universal of "jar" (*ghaṭajāti*) and so forth would possess the status of being a relation.
Alternatively, if it is said that those things which produce the cognition of a relation are called "relations," [then...]
In that case, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that even the eyes and so forth would possess the status of being a relation.

If, on the other hand, a relation is defined as that which is determined by the cognition of a relation, then there would be the undesirable consequence that even in the case of dogs, elephants, children, and the like, they would possess the status of being a relation when the word "relation" is applied to them.
If the related object and its other correlate share the status of being objects of a single cognition, it follows that the other must possess the nature of the relation itself.
Alternatively, if the relation is the form of the relation,
then there would be the undesirable consequence of its being non-different from conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
As for the objection that the intermediate form of the "courtesan" (gaṇikā) is not a differentiator, the refutation has already been stated previously.
Furthermore, in this case, the cognition "the cloth is in these threads" is determined by the notion of "here" (iha), because the notion of "here" consists in the awareness of a locus.

Furthermore, it is not logical to postulate something else when another form is being perceived, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is argued that it is assimilated by means of the cognition of inherence (*samavāya*),
that too is untenable.
Because the cognition of inherence is not possible;
people never perceive it such that they think, "This is the thread, this is the cloth, and this is the inherence of these two.
Or, if it is inferred by means of inference:
There are two types of inference: the perceived (*dṛṣṭa*) and that which is perceived through generality (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*).
There is no [inference] based on what is not perceived, because that would be distinct from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Nor does that which is perceived through generality exist.
Because its effect, which would arise from it, is not perceived.

[Objection: But surely the cognition "here" itself is the indicator of inherence; the notion "the cloth is here in these threads" is caused by a relation, because it is an uncontradicted cognition of "here," like the cognition "curd is here in the bowl."
What is inferred by this?
Is it merely a cause, or is it a relationship?
If it is merely a cause, [then...]
Therefore, it should be understood as something already established and proven.
Now, as for the relation: is it conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*)?
There would be the loss of the acceptance of inference based on conjunction (*saṃyoga*);
in the case of inference based on inherence (*samavāya*), there would be the absence of a [logical] relation.
Furthermore, one thing cannot be the indicator (*gamaka*) of another when they stand in a relation with something else, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Never has it been observed that Yajñadatta’s sense organ, by virtue of its commonality as an instrument, reveals an object such as color to Devadatta’s eye when they are unrelated.
This being so, one must consider how the systematic arrangement of substances and other categories can exist in the absence of universals (*sāmānya*) and inherence (*samavāya*). [Objection:
It is known that there is no deviation because the water obtained from that lineage [is the same].
That is incorrect, because the final composite substances lack the capacity to produce [further effects]; moreover,
there is no plurality among the individual instances of water.
And how it does not exist has already been explained previously (1.13b).

Furthermore, is the non-deviation of the previously mentioned cognition made known by the capacity for purposeful action (*pravṛtti-sāmarthya*) acting as a logical mark (*liṅga*), or is it by means of the nature of direct perception (*adhyakṣa*) itself?
If it is by means of a logical mark, [then...]
That is incorrect, because no relationship with that [word] is apprehended; or, if it were apprehended, there would be no need for the efficacy of purposeful activity.
Now,
if it is argued that [the cognition] consists of direct perception, that is incorrect, because there is no sensory contact with that which has already ceased as previously described.
The cognition of that object is not the result of direct perception, because it lacks a real objective basis (*nirālambanatva*), like the perception of a mass of hair or similar illusions.
It is neither the non-existence of the cognition that appears, nor is it the existence [of the object], because that [object] is absent.

The meaning of "object" for that which is non-existent must be stated: is it by way of imparting a form, or by being endowed with properties such as magnitude, or by mere existence, or by simultaneous arising?
Since everything has been refuted, how can this be an object?
If it were an object, one would have to seek the cause of falsity in the cognition of a mass of hair and the like.
If falsity were established by the mere existence of a self, it would follow that everything is false;
consequently, there would be a collapse of all reality.

Alternatively, if non-erroneousness is apprehended—such that the cognition produced through the connection of the self and the internal organ is manifested as being characterized by non-erroneousness—[then the self exists].
That is incorrect.
That non-deviation is either a property of that [object], or its essential nature.
If it were a property of that [object],...
Is it permanent or impermanent?
If it is permanent,
then it should be understood as being refuted by the fault of [the theory of] birth.
Now, if it is impermanent, was it produced before, simultaneously with, or after [the cause]?
If, first of all, it were produced before,
In that case, whose is this property (*dharma*)?
For a property cannot exist without a substratum (*dharmī*).
Since its form is differentiated from everything else, it must be stated: "Whose is it? and "Of whom does it belong?"
Now, if [the cognition] arises simultaneously [with the object], it must be stated what the relationship between the two is;

for in the absence of the relationships of identity (*tādātmya*), origination from that (*tadutpatti*), or inherence (*samavāya*), the meaning of the genitive case must be explained as its non-deviation (*avyabhicāritva*). If, on the other hand, [the cognition] arises subsequently, then the deviation of the cognition was already established previously.
[It] follows [that there is no such thing].

Furthermore, there exists no internal phenomenon (*dharma*) that is non-deviant in nature and distinct from pleasure and so forth, because such a thing is not admitted by [the opponent] himself due to the impossibility of its being perceived.

Furthermore, if non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) and the other [criteria] are admitted to be distinct entities (*dharmārthāntara*), it is proclaimed that cognition delimited by them establishes the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
But this is untenable,
because it is impossible for a single cognition to persist at the time of its apprehension while being delimited by multiple qualifiers individually.
In the absence of both the object to be known and the means of knowing, there would be a cognition connected solely to the agent.
(1.142) Now, as for its essential nature— its non-deviation— is that due to conformity with its own mere existence, or due to conformity with the existence of another object?
If, then, non-deviation is said to consist merely in the existence of cognition, then even the cognition of a mass of hair would be non-deviant.
Furthermore, a cognition is not designated as deviant or non-deviant solely on the basis of the existence of that cognition.
Now, does this non-deviation depend upon the existence of another entity that provides no assistance, or does it depend upon the existence of another entity that does provide assistance?
If it were by depending on the existence of another entity that provides no assistance,
then it would follow that even the cognitions of a mass of hair or two moons would possess non-deviation.

Now, regarding the non-deviation [of a reason] based on the existence of an auxiliary that is a distinct entity: is it due to the existence of an auxiliary for a distinct entity that is being perceived, or is it due to the existence of an auxiliary for a distinct entity that is the opposite of that?

If the former were accepted as the position, then there would be no non-deviation for the inferential cognition of the past and future, nor for the yogic perception, nor for the cognition produced by the words of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*).
Because there would be no purpose served by understanding that [meaning],
or else it would follow that the act of spreading [the canopy] would be omitted. Now, if the latter view is held, then:
It follows that the cognition of a mass of hair or of two moons would be non-erroneous; thus, [the opponent's position] is grasped incorrectly.
Furthermore, is that cognition known to be non-erroneous by means of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) as a cognizer, or is it unknown?
If it is known, is its knowledge of the nature of self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvid-rūpa*), or is it cognizable by another cognition (*jñānāntara-vedya*)?
Therefore, if it were understood as having the nature of self-cognition,
that would be incorrect, because [the opponent] does not admit this himself.
Or, if you do accept this, it contradicts your own tenet.
Furthermore, if you maintain that [the object] is cognizable by another cognition,
then the basis for the distinction between the two cognitions must be sought.
Knowledge is distinguished from that which has the form of non-knowledge by its nature as knowledge;
but how is it distinguished from other cognitions?
Is it distinguished by its nature as knowledge, or rather by a different form?
If it [the object] is excluded by virtue of having the nature of cognition,
then the nature of cognition is removed from other things, such as water and so forth;
or else, [it is excluded] by means of another form.
If another form were admitted, there would be an absence of the form of cognition,
because it is impossible for two forms to be identical;
and if they were identical, that single entity would have to be either cognition or non-cognition.
If it is cognition,
then it does not exclude itself through another form,
but rather solely by its very nature as cognition.
Otherwise, it would follow that everything else is of the nature of ignorance. If ignorance is established, then our desired position is proven.
Or, [if you argue that] it is knowledge...
Regarding that which differentiates,
it should be understood according to what was previously stated as to by what it is differentiated;
furthermore, it is not possible for it to be cognizable by another consciousness.
If it is not cognized,
how then do you know that it exists?
By this very same path, one must admit the absence of distinction between the cognition of reality and the cognition of what is other than reality.
Therefore, the term "non-erroneous" (*avyabhicāri*) is redundant;
it is also redundant because [such errors] have already been excluded by the phrase "contact between sense-faculty and object" (*indriyārthasannikarṣa*).
For there is no arising of contact between the eye and an object in the cognition of a mass of hair (*keśoṇḍuka*).
[Objection: Surely there exists the cognition of water in a mirage;
for its removal, the term "non-erroneous" (*avyabhicāri*) is employed. [Reply:
That is not so, because what appears is water.
And there is no connection with that;
it is connected with what exists, not with what does not exist.

Or, even if there were a connection with that [sunlight], it would not be logical for the cognition having that as its object to be false here, just like the perception of real water. Now, although there is no connection of the eye with the water being perceived,
nevertheless, by taking the mirage as its objective support (*ālambana*)...
There is a connection with the collection, because that alone is the objective support, since [the cognition] proceeds toward that location.
Therefore, falsity consists in this: that the object of apprehension (*ālambana*) is one thing, yet something else appears.
What, then, is this so-called "object of apprehension" by virtue of which it is proclaimed that "the object of apprehension is one thing and what appears is another"?

Is it the state of being the producer of consciousness (*vijñāna*), the state of imparting its form (*ākāra*), the state of being the locus of consciousness, or the state of being manifested by consciousness?

If, therefore, being a producer of consciousness is the meaning of "object-condition" (ālambana), then it would follow that the eye, light, and so forth would also possess the status of an object-condition. Alternatively, if being an object-condition means imparting a form (ākāra) [to consciousness], [then...]
That is incorrect, because it is not accepted in the system of the Naiyāyikas;
and we shall demonstrate later on how the form of the object is not logically possible in consciousness.
Now, if being the substratum of consciousness constitutes being the objective support (*ālambana*), then cognition does not arise as something projected upon a circle of mirages;
rather, it attains a self that is inherent within itself.
Now, if it is the case that the object is that which is illuminated by consciousness, then in the case of the cognition of water, water would be perceived,
and not the mirage-rays.
Now, if mirages are perceived as having the form of water,
is that form of water distinct from the mirages or non-distinct?
If it were non-distinct, [then...]
Is it real or unreal?
If it is real, how can there be falsity in the cognition of it? Or if it is unreal, then [that is the case].
It would follow that even the rays of light lack ultimate reality (*atāttvikatva*).
If they are identical with water that lacks ultimate reality, what is meant by saying that the cognition of that water is "not true"?
It means that the cognition of the rays of light is not true.
And when a single form of water is being perceived, who has told this to the "Beloved of the Gods" (devānāmpriya): that it is rays of light appearing?
Or, if [the rays] were a different entity altogether, then it should not be said that "rays of light appear in the form of water."
Mirages are separated from the appearance of water.
Now, in the cognition of a mass of hair, what appears? What is its objective support?

Just as the hair-tuft itself is both the objective support (*ālambana*) and that which is perceived, so too is the water itself both the objective support and that which is perceived; no other objective support should be postulated.
Nor is the cognition of water false by virtue of having something other than the perceived water as its object; rather, it is false because [the object] lacks ultimate reality.
Otherwise, even the cognition of a mass of hair would not be considered false.
Because it is distinct from having any other object.
1.1a2 Furthermore, as for what was said— that the mirage-region is the object because one moves toward the mirage-rays—
if that is so, then by this same reasoning, the location [of the rays] would also logically be established as the object.

Furthermore, it is not tenable that the cognition of water arises from a sense-object contact with an object distinct from the appearance [of water], because such a thing is not observed in the case of a cognition of real water;
otherwise, even the cognition of fire inferred [from smoke] would result in being produced by sense-object contact.
Because it arises from the contact between the self and the mind.
Now, if there is no connection of the mind with the fire that is being perceived,
then here too, there is no connection of the eye with the water that is being perceived.

Therefore, the term "non-erroneous" (*avyabhicārin*) is not appropriate, because its purpose is already served by the phrase "contact between sense-faculty and object" (*indriyārthasannikarṣa*). Furthermore, it is untenable for this reason as well: because there can be no cognition of that which is to be excluded (*apohya*).
If it is argued that the term is employed with the desire to exclude the cognition of water in a mirage (*marīcyudaka-vijñāna*), [we reply: ...
How then is it removed?
Because its object, water, does not exist.
If it is non-existent, [how can it be removed?]
What is the meaning of "object" (viṣaya)? One should follow what was stated previously:
if water appears therein, [it is the object].
How is it that it does not exist?
It is true that it appears;
however, it appears as something unreal.
What is non-reality (*atathyatā*)?
Is it the absence of that which is being perceived, or is it that very perception itself which is non-existent?
If it is the absence of that which is being perceived, [then...]
Does that occur at that very moment or after some interval of time?
If it occurs at that very moment,
is it cognized or uncognized?
If it has been cognized, by what is it cognized?
Is it by the cognition of water, or by another cognition?
If it is [known] by means of the cognition of water, that is not so, because that [cognition] has water as its object.

Alternatively, if that [non-existence] were its object, then it would not be tenable to call the cognition of water "erroneous," because that which has non-existence as its object must exist in the ultimate sense. Furthermore, in a consciousness that apprehends the form of water, the cessation of water does not appear; for if it did, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Nor can it be established by another cognition, because the simultaneous occurrence of two cognitions is impossible.

Furthermore, if the determination of non-existence were made by a cognition of non-existence, and the determination of existence by a cognition of existence, [then there would be an infinite regress].
Then the existence and non-existence of that water would occur at the same time.
Or, if the cognition of existence does not establish existence while the cognition of non-existence establishes non-existence—
oh, what a royal decree this is for the beast of a Naiyāyika!
And if the cognition of an entity does not establish the status of that entity,
then there would follow the consequence of a lack of confidence regarding all entities;
and when that consequence follows, even non-existence would lack stability.
And if that [existence] were not established, there would be a collapse of reality.
Furthermore, if it is unperceived, how do you know again that "it exists"?
Furthermore, at another time, nothing is sublated,
because even that which is real water can be shown to be non-existent at another time.
1.1b2 Now, if non-existence itself is being perceived, how can the falsity of the cognition having that as its object be established,
given that the very non-existence which is being perceived is logically consistent?
Furthermore, when a positive entity (*bhāva*) is being perceived, it is not logical to conceive of it as non-existent, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Otherwise, one would have to conceive of taste and so forth while form (*rūpa*) and the like are being perceived;
yet this is not done.
In the same way, water is also perceived here;
indeed it is perceived,
but it is unreal.
If this is so, then this is a conceptual proliferation regarding water, just as one speaks of "long water" or "sweet water.
Is it not the case that in all these states water is perceived, and by means of that perception, the designation "water" is applied to them?
If that is so, then here too, in both states, water is perceived— both real water and unreal water.
In the cognition of real water, real water appears,
not unreal water nor the absence of water.
Thus, when there is the cognition of water in what is not water, it is that which is not water which appears,
and not real water or the absence of water;
for cognitions are restricted to their own respective objects.
1.1b Now, if it is argued that falsity consists in being sublated (*bādhyamānatva*), is it the object that is sublated, the cognition, or both?
1.1ba1 If it is the sublation of the object, [then...]
By what is it sublated?
Does it sublate itself, or by another entity, such as cognition?
If it sublates itself, [then...]
In that case, is the sublation performed by it or made known?
If it is performed,
is it distinct from [the object] or non-distinct?
If it were non-distinct [from itself],
then it would be produced by itself as an act of self-sublation;
and that is not possible, because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself.
Now, if it is argued that [the agent] is distinct [from the action], even so, agency belongs to that which already exists;
there is no denial of what is perceived.
Now, if sublation is being made known,
is that [sublation] non-different or different [from the object]?
If it is non-different,
In that case, what is it that is made known by that sublation? Is water being made known? Or is it something else?
If it is distinct [from water], then...
Thus, the fact that the indicator exists is established, as is the existence of that which is being perceived.
Even if it is sublated by another object, nevertheless, the relationship between the sublated and the sublator exists between two existing things, like that between a subject and a king.

Furthermore, the relationship of the sublated and the sublator is not possible for a single entity. What is done by that [sublation] to that which is being perceived—is it produced or is it made known? If it is produced, is it distinct or non-distinct [from the object]? If it is non-distinct, [then...]
In that case, what would be meant by saying that something non-different [from the water] is produced?
It is water that is produced;
and with its production, the cognition of it is no longer false.
Now, even if it is produced as something distinct, nevertheless, because it is perceived as being connected with water, the existence of water is established;
for never is the conventional usage of "Devadatta's eyes" established in the absence of Devadatta.
Now, if it is being made known,
is it non-different or different [from the object]?
If it is made known as non-different, [then...]
In that case, what is it that is made known by that [cognition] which constitutes the sublation? Is it water that is made known?
Or is it something distinct [from the cognition] that is made known?
Nevertheless, since this sublation of water appears as being dependent on something else, its absolute non-existence is not established.
Therefore, sublation is not possible even by means of another object.
Now, if it is sublated by a cognition, is that [cognition] one whose object is the same, one whose object is different, or one that is objectless?
If [the sublating cognition] has that same object,
then it establishes its true nature and does not subvert it, because its form terminates in that very appearance;
but if the sublating cognition has a different object, [it cannot subvert the first].
That too is not tenable;
for whatever has a particular object as its domain establishes the existence of that very object alone, but it is neither an establisher nor a negator of anything else.
For cognitions terminate within their own respective objects.
Now, if it were sublated by something that lacks an object,
it would neither affirm nor negate anything precisely because of its lack of an object.

1.1ba2 Now, if cognition is sublated, what is its sublation? Is it in the form of the exclusion of its own nature, or in the form of the denial of its own nature, or characterized by the removal of its object?
Therefore, if sublation consists in the exclusion of its own nature, then everything would be sublated,
because one cognition is being set aside by another cognition.
If, on the other hand, it consists in the denial of its own nature, that is incorrect,
because even the cognition of illusory water is being experienced.
Now, if it is argued that sublation (*bādha*) is characterized by the removal of the object (*viṣayāpahāra*),
that too is not tenable;
for it has just been explained how such a removal of the object cannot be effected.
1.1b. If it is not sublated, why does this entity not perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)? What is this causal efficiency that is not accomplished by it for persons?
Is it in the form of cognition, or in the form of activity, or in the form of attainment, or in the form of the production and experience of pleasure and pain?
Therefore, if it does not perform the causal function characterized by consciousness,
that would be illogical;
for water certainly performs the causal function characterized by consciousness.
Now, if one does not perform that which has the nature of activity, that is improper;
for activity indeed conforms to the desire of the person.
It does not follow that the existence or non-existence of the nature of an object is established [by this];
for a person may or may not act according to their desire,
yet the non-existence of that object is not proven by that much alone.
If it does not perform a purposeful action (arthakriyā) in the form of attainment, then it would follow that it is non-existent;
however, that too is incorrect.
Because existence is possible even in the absence of contact with the moon, sun, planets, constellations, stars, and so forth; furthermore,

if it does not perform a causal function (arthakriyā) in the form of pleasure or pain, does it fail to produce the pleasure born of seeing [them], or rather the pleasure born of connection with the body?
If it does not produce that which is born of vision, that is incorrect; for it certainly does produce it.
Or, if it does not produce that which is born of connection with the body, [that too is incorrect].
In that case, there would be an inconsistency regarding the moon, sun, planets, constellations, and so forth;
for although they exist, they do not produce pleasure arising from connection with a body.
Nor is there non-existence of things by virtue of their not performing causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*),
because they arise from their own causes merely as the production of cognition, or else they do not act due to the absence of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*).
Furthermore, does it not perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) for one cognizer or for all cognizers?
If it does not perform causal efficiency for one cognizer, then its non-existence [is established];
however, in that case, there would be a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the moon, sun, planets, lunar mansions, and stars.
And regarding the case of one about to die:
if it does not perform a causal function for all cognizers, then it would follow that it is non-existent;
if that were so, then it would follow that all entities are non-existent.
For not all things are causes for every human purpose,
nor can it be understood by one of limited vision that this [word] is devoid of the performance of any human purpose;
therefore, it remains established that the term "non-deviant" (avyabhicārin) is meaningless.
c. Others, however, maintain that the cognition of water in a mirage is of the nature of memory (smṛti), not of the nature of error (bhrānti). How can that [cognition] be considered memory?

Does [the status of being a memory] arise by virtue of being a grasping of water, or by virtue of being a grasping of water that was previously grasped, or by virtue of occurring at a time subsequent to the grasping of water, or by virtue of being objectless, or by virtue of arising in the form "that which I saw"?
If it were by virtue of being a grasping of water, then it would follow that all cognitions of water are memories.
If, on the other hand, its status as a memory is due to being a grasping of water that was previously grasped, [then...]

In that case, even the first [cognition] would entail being a memory (smṛti) because it apprehends water already apprehended, since there is no difference in its apprehending what has been previously grasped. Alternatively, if the first cognition does not have the apprehension of water already grasped, then there is a difference in their objects (bhinnaviṣayatva).
Furthermore, if they have different objects, the second [cognition] loses its status as apprehending what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhitva*).

If, on the other hand, they have the same object, then it follows that even the first [cognition] is apprehending what has already been apprehended, because it consists in the apprehension of an object no different [from the previous one], just like the subsequent cognition.
Just as the nature of the cognition of blue does not differ among multiple cognitions that arise simultaneously and grasp a single specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of blue, so it is here as well.
Likewise, it follows that successive cognitions (dhārāvāhivijñāna) would have the nature of memory;
similarly, recognition (pratyabhijñāna) would entail being a form of memory because it grasps what has already been grasped.
Now, if recognition does not possess the quality of apprehending an object already apprehended, then its status as recognition ceases;
for the initial perception does not arise with the thought, "This is that very same [object]."
Likewise, even inferential cognition (anumānika-vijñāna) would incur the status of memory because it apprehends an object already grasped.
If, on the other hand, its status as memory is due to its occurring at a time subsequent to the apprehension of water,
then it follows that the mental impression (saṃskāra) itself must take the form of memory.
Furthermore, because the perception of taste occurs at a time subsequent to the grasping of water,
it is incorrect to claim that it is of the nature of memory on the grounds that it lacks a [present] object.
How can that which arises as the cognizer of the form of an object made known by a prior experience be said to be without an object (*nirviṣayatva*)?
If it is argued that it is objectless because the previously experienced object has ceased and no object exists at the same time [as the cognition],
then [the same would apply to] that which is produced by an injunction (*codanā*).
Because knowledge would lack an object, it would result in being a mere memory, since the object in the form of something to be done (kartavyatā) would then be absent;
or, even if it were present, its nature as something to be done would be untenable.
If that were untenable, it would follow that the performance of the seven-threaded sacrifice (saptatantukriyā) would be abolished.
Furthermore, if memory were defined by its lack of an object,
then the recollection of existing things such as jars or universals (jāti) would result in the absurdity of not being considered memory.
The claim that its status as memory is established by its arising in the form "then I saw" is incorrect;
for how can that which arises in the form "there is water here" possess the nature of being "I saw"?
Now, if this [cognition] arises through such a mode of being "deprived," what indeed is this so-called deprivation (*vipramoṣa*)?

Is it the appropriation of the form of experience, or the destruction of the form of recollection, or the apprehension of a previously unknown object, or its being produced by the contact of sense-organ and object, or its not being produced by the contact of sense-organ and object?
Therefore, if it were to assume the form of direct experience, then its nature as recollection would not be tenable;
yet, if it is of the nature of recollection, [it cannot be the apprehension of that object].
In that case, the assumption of the form of the experience is not tenable,
because the forms of memory and experience are characterized by their mutual exclusion.
Alternatively, [if one were to argue] that it is the destruction of the form of the memory...
That is incorrect,
because consciousness itself is admitted to be memory;
for cessation (pradhvaṃsa) is non-conscious in nature.
How does it establish the nature of memory?

If it is argued that the "loss of memory" (smṛtipramoṣa) refers to the apprehension of an object not previously experienced, then the cognitions of things such as gold or a jackfruit— which have never been experienced at all— would result in being classified as cases of lost memory.

If it is argued that the state of being a lapse of memory (*smṛtivipramoṣa*) consists in arising from the contact of a sense-organ with its object, then it follows as an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that all cognitions would be lapses of memory.
Alternatively, if it is argued that the state of being a lapse of memory consists in not arising from the contact of a sense-organ with its object—
In that case, it would follow that cognition produced by an injunction, as well as inferential and analogical cognitions, are merely lapses of memory.
Therefore, the more one examines this lapse of memory, the more it fails to withstand logical scrutiny.
Consequently, the cognition of water in a mirage does not consist of a lapse of memory.
Rather, it would be either a case of erroneous cognition (*viparītakhyāti*) or correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
Likewise, the term "determinate in nature" (*vyavasāyātmaka*) need not be included, as there is nothing to be excluded [by it].

But surely, regarding an object such as a post, when there is contact between the sense organ and the object, a cognition of doubt arises from the perception of the mere universal while the particular is not perceived?
That is removed.
When that doubtful cognition has arisen, does something appear or not appear? If it appears, [then...]
Is that [object] a property-bearer (dharmin) or a property (dharma)? If it appears as a property-bearer,
is it real (tāttvika) or unreal (atāttvika)?
If it were real, there would be no removal of the cognition whose object it is; if, however, it were unreal, [there would be].

In that case, since [the possibility of error] has already been excluded by the term "non-deviating" (*avyabhicāri*), the term "of the nature of ascertainment" (*vyavasāyātmaka*) need not be employed.
Now, if a property (*dharma*) appears, it must be either characterized as a post (*sthāṇutva*), characterized as a person (*puruṣatva*), or both.
In that case, if the property characterized as being a post appears,
it must be either real or unreal.
If it is real, [then...]
How can that cognition have the nature of doubt,
given that it has the nature of apprehending a real object, like the perception of actual water? Or, if it is not real...
In that case, since [the possibility of error] has already been excluded by the term "non-deviant" (*avyabhicāri*), the term "of the nature of ascertainment" (*vyavasāyātmaka*) need not be employed.
Now, if a property characterized as "humanity" (*puruṣatva*) appears,
is that [property] real (*tāttvika*) or unreal (*atāttvika*)?
If it were real, how could that cognition have the nature of doubt? Or if it were unreal, [how could it produce certainty]?
In that case, because it has already been excluded by the term "non-erroneous" (*avyabhicārin*), the term "of the nature of determinate judgment" (*vyavasāyātmaka*) is not more effective.
Now, if both appear [to be true], then both must be either real or unreal; or else, one must be real and the other unreal.
Therefore, if both are real, then that cognition must itself be real;
it cannot consist of doubt.
If, moreover, both are unreal,
then that cognition is of the nature of error, not of the nature of doubt.
Now, if one [cognition] is real and the other is unreal, then that very same cognition would be erroneous and that very same [cognition] would be non-erroneous;
it would be erroneous because its nature consists in grasping an unreal object.
It is non-erroneous because it consists in the apprehension of the real object;
by this, the cognition of a double moon is excluded,
for in that case, the form of a substance appears.
It does not have the form of a quality.
If it is argued that doubt-cognition is that which appears as the form of a doubtful object, then does such a doubtful object exist or not?
If that [doubt] exists,
how can its cognition be of the nature of doubt, given that it consists in the apprehension of an object that is not sublated, like the cognition of real water?
Or, if it does not exist, [how can there be such a cognition]?
In that case, since [the definition] has already been excluded by the term "non-erroneous" (*avyabhicārin*), the term "of the nature of ascertainment" (*vyavasāyātmaka*) is redundant.
Alternatively, if nothing at all appears [to consciousness],
then it cannot be produced by the contact of the sense organ with its object, just like the cognition of illusory water.
Therefore, the term "of the nature of ascertainment" (*vyavasāyātmaka*) is also not to be accepted.
Furthermore, the term "inexpressible" (*avyapadeśya*) is not more valid than others; this should be seen in the *Lakṣaṇasāra*.
Likewise, being "born from the contact of the sense-organ and the object" (*indriyārthasannikarṣaja*) is also untenable, because there is no means of perceiving that [contact].

1.41 For the contact between the sense organ and its object is either indicated by the non-perception of obstructed objects, or indicated by an obstruction, or is to be determined by the cognition of jars and so forth produced by that contact.
If it were indicated by the non-perception of obstructed objects,
that would be incorrect.
Because a relationship with it is impossible, and because non-apprehension is observed even in its absence;
for how can that whose existence occurs even when another is absent indicate the existence of that other?
Now, as for the mark of obscuration,
that is incorrect, because there is no connection with it.
Because it is observed to exist even in the absence of that [object],
or else, if it existed when that [object] was present, its obscuration would be purposeless;
how then could there be cognition of it in the absence of that [object]?

If it is argued that this is understood through the cognition of its existence, its jar-ness, and so forth, that is incorrect; for as long as those [properties] are not cognized, its being produced from them cannot be cognized.
This contact is comparable to a goblin, an atom, or Maheśvara.
How is its dependence [upon the object] known in cognition?
And how does cognition make known that contact between the sense-organ and the object?
Is it by way of having the form of consciousness, or by way of having the form of the effect, or by way of having the form produced by the contact of the sense-faculty and the object?
If it were by way of being the intrinsic nature of cognition, that would be incorrect.

Even in the absence of that [external object], the form of cognition is possible in cognitions such as those of comparison (*upamāna*) and so forth. Furthermore, if it is argued that [the object] is made known by virtue of being the effect [of the cognition],
that too is incorrect.
Because that [inference] exists in cases such as analogical cognition and the perception of water in a mirage or blue color;
for how can something that exists without another be called a "cognizer" of that other?
Otherwise, even existence (*sattva*) and other such properties would be indicative [of the object].

If it is argued that it indicates [the object] by virtue of having a form produced by the contact of the sense-organ with the object (*indriyārthasannikarṣajanyākāratayā*), then is this form produced by the contact of the sense-organ with the object non-different from the form of the cognition, or is it different?
If it were non-distinct [from cognition], then it would be merely the nature of cognition itself,
and there would be no other discernible form distinct from it, as is the case in inferential and other types of cognitions.
Alternatively, if there is an excess of another form, its nature as cognition is lost; or if it is distinct [from cognition],
then that [distinct entity] alone must be the means of communication.
Nor [is it the case] for the form of the cognition itself;
for that too lacks the capacity to inform [us], because it is not cognized by itself.
Furthermore, the consciousness produced from the contact of the sense faculty and the object must be apprehended in its own essential nature.
From that, there is the recollection of pervasion; following that, the cognition of reflective awareness (parāmarśa);
and from that, the comprehension of the object to be inferred. Yet, consciousness does not maintain its state for such a long duration.
Because it has been set aside due to its having been cultivated as impure;
or, if inference is conceptualized according to the principle of the property-bearer and the property as mounted upon the intellect, then it becomes non-real, like the inference of the Sugata.
1.42 Likewise, it is also untenable that [cognition] is produced by the sense organs, because no production by the sense organs is perceived apart from [the cognition itself].
Cognition is cognized precisely as its own intrinsic nature, not through any other form.
Alternatively, if that [object] were made known [by the cognition], it would follow that the cognition is devoid of an aspect (ākāra).
Furthermore, cognition is not observed to be connected with the sense organ, such that its perception could lead to the inference of the sense organ.
Now, action is observed elsewhere to be accomplished by an instrument;
let that very action be the mover, whose connection with an instrument is already understood.
Furthermore, it is not possible for one thing to be the indicator (*gamaka*) of another through a relationship with something else merely on the basis of some similarity;

for never has it been observed that when there is a connection between Devadatta’s eye and the color blue, Yajñadatta’s sense organ reveals objects such as a jar due to the similarity of their being instruments, even though no such [causal] connection exists.
In the same manner, the form produced by the object (*arthajanyākāra*) within consciousness should also be understood as refuted by this very same reasoning.

1.43 Likewise, does the object also produce consciousness by having produced an excellence (*atiśaya*) or not having produced an excellence; and if it produces [it] by having produced an excellence, is that excellence non-distinct [from the object] or distinct?
If it acts while not having produced an excellence, then it would either always act or never act at all.
Neither agency nor non-agency would be possible, because there would be no departure from its own nature.
Likewise, even if an excellence (*atiśaya*) were produced that is non-different [from the agent], it would not act, because the form of the non-agent persists within it.
Or, if there is no such persistence, then the excellence is not non-different from it.
Now, if it is produced by something that has acquired an excellence distinct [from itself], even so it is not tenable, because it does not transcend its non-productive nature;
or, if it does transcend it, then momentariness follows.
Consequently, it follows that consciousness produced by the contact of a sense faculty with its object is not the definition of perception.
[Chapter 2: Examination of the Mīmāṃsā Definition of Valid Cognition:
Others, however, state the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as being that which apprehends an object not already known.
However, they should be regarded as proponents of an untenable position.

If it is asked how their position is untenable, it is said: although there is no difference in the nature of the apprehension of a single object as it actually exists among cognitions produced by distinct causal factors, the validity belongs to the cognition that arose first, and not to the subsequent one.
In this regard, a restrictive principle must be stated:

2.1 Now, even though there is no difference in their both having the nature of apprehending an object as it is established, validity is established for the previously arisen cognition, and not for the subsequent cognition.

Then, by this very same reasoning, the lack of authority (aprāmāṇya) of the first [cognition] would also follow, because there is no difference in its being the apprehension of an object already apprehended.

Just as among multiple cognitions of blue that arise simultaneously and manifest the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of a single blue object, their nature as the apprehension of the same object—blue—is not distinct;
likewise, the nature of subsequent cognitions arising before and after will not cease from being the apprehension of an object already apprehended.

Now, regarding the restriction of the object for the preceding and succeeding cognitions: the previously arisen cognition is apprehended by way of assuming the form of an object not yet apprehended, whereas the subsequent one arises having as its object a form of an object already apprehended.
If it has as its object an object already grasped, how can there be a restriction of the object?
Now, how can there be the grasping of an already grasped object if it has a restricted object,
given the contradiction between having a restricted object and grasping what has already been grasped?
And if it has a restricted object, [how can it grasp what is already grasped?]
Therefore, both [cognitions] possess validity because there is no difference in their being apprehenders of an object not previously known.
Alternatively, if they have the same object,
then both possess either validity or invalidity because there is no difference in their apprehending what has already been apprehended.
Thus, for those who long for the authority of the Śruti, this occurrence—resembling the maxim of "the entry of a goitre and the exit of the pupil"—is difficult to resolve.

(2.11) Now, even if it were granted that [Smṛti] possesses authority despite its object already being known, would not the authority of Smṛti itself follow, or else the status of being a fruit of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphalatā*)?
Who is there to prevent this?
Recollection arising here must have as its object either the form of the object made known by a previous experience, or another object, or be without an object.

If it has as its object the form of the object made known by the previously mentioned experience, then its status as the fruit of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot be denied, because— as has been stated— there is no difference in its being the apprehension of an object already grasped.
In this way, a seventh means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) called "recollection" (smṛti) would result for the Mīmāṃsakas.
Now, if it has as its object a thing not previously determined by a prior cognition,
how can its status as the fruit of a means of valid cognition be removed?
Furthermore, it would not attain the nature of memory, just like the initial experience itself;
for memory has as its object things that have been seen or heard, not objects that have not been apprehended.
If, on the other hand, it is maintained that memory is without an object, [then it would be indistinguishable from non-cognition].
In that case, the lack of authority (aprāmāṇya) of memory is not due to its grasping an object already grasped, but rather due to its being devoid of an object, like the cognition of a mass of hair.
Furthermore, if it were devoid of an object, [it would be invalid].
In that case, how can it be said that it grasps an object already grasped?
If you say it grasps an object already grasped, then it cannot be said to be without an object.
Nor are they devoid of objects; for memories terminate in the forms of objects made known by prior experience, such as "I have served my mother and father" or "I have five servants."
Because through the cognition of memory (*smṛtijñāna*), there appears the form of an object that was made known by a previous experience.
Now, at the time of the cognitive state of memory, since the object that was previously taken as the domain of awareness has vanished, it cannot have that [vanished object] as its objective domain.
Thus, it has been stated that the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of memory is due to its being without an objective domain (*nirviṣayatva*), and not because it grasps an object already grasped.

2.2 Furthermore, if it were established that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose object is already determined is not a valid cognition, then inferential knowledge would consequently fall into the state of being invalid.
How so?

Is it said that one understands through inference that very same generality of fire (*agnitvasāmānya*) which was determined at the time of grasping the relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) as residing non-deviantly (*ajahadvṛtti*) in the inferential mark (*liṅga*) by means of perception; or rather, does one understand the essential nature of the fire, or the possessive sense (*matvartha*), or the existence [of the fire] simultaneous with the operation of the inferential mark,
or the subordination of the generality of fire to the inferential mark, or the dependence of the generality of fire upon the individual fire (*agnivyakti*)?

2.21 If it is admitted that [the cognition] has as its object a generality already previously determined, then it does not attain validity at all, because it grasps an object already grasped, just like memory.
Since it lacks validity, the establishment of the presence of fire is not possible.
And since that [fire] is not established, there can be no establishment of a particular fire through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
Consequently, there would be an absence of all worldly transactions such as, "There is fire over there; let fire be brought."

Now, if it is argued that this would result in the loss of conventional practice (*vyavahāra*), and that one must therefore admit the validity of inference even regarding an object already previously determined,
then the qualification "cognizing an object not yet apprehended" (*anadhigatārthagantṛ*) is useless for the Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*).
(2.22) Now, if you intend to infer the essential nature of fire (*pāvakasvarūpa*), [then...]
Therefore, has that [object] been previously ascertained by way of the non-abandonment of its defining characteristic (*liṅga*), or not?
If it was previously perceived, then inference would have for its object something already known.
But if it was not previously perceived, [then inference would be invalid].
If fire is not pervasive [of the mountain], then it must be cognized through inference;
if that is accepted, it would follow that inference could also apply to grass, water, and so forth.
Alternatively, if it is the possessive sense (*matvartha*) that is inferred, [then...]
Was that [object] previously ascertained or not?
If it was ascertained, how can the qualification "that which makes known an object not already apprehended" apply to inference?
If, on the other hand, it is not apprehended at all, then it has been stated that the consequence would follow that there could even be inference regarding objects such as water or grass (2.24).
Now, if it is argued that the existence of the universal "fire-ness" (*agnitva-sāmānya*) is inferred at the same time as the operation of the inferential mark (*liṅga*), [we reply:]...
That existence which is simultaneous with the operation of inference is either distinct from or non-distinct from the generality of fire-ness (*agnitva-sāmānya*).
If it is non-distinct,
then at that time, the inference would have as its object only the existence previously perceived.
How could the qualification "one who cognizes an object not previously apprehended" not be meaningless?
Furthermore, if it is distinct [from the cognition],
is that [object] one previously perceived or unperceived?

If that [fire] was previously perceived, then it is not tenable for inference to have that as its object, because the qualification "apprehending an unapprehended object" would fail. If, on the other hand, it was not perceived,
how can something like water be inferred by means of smoke?
2.25 Now, if the subordination to the mark (*liṅga*) of the generality of fire-ness (*agnitva-sāmānya*) is apprehended through inference,
is that subordination to the mark distinct from or non-distinct from the generality of fire-ness?
If it is non-distinct, then inference would have as its object only the previously perceived generality of fire-ness.
How does it possess validity?
Now, if it is distinct [from the probandum],
was it ascertained at the time of grasping the relationship of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) as being the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of the mark (*liṅga*), or not?
If it has already been determined, how can inference have as its object a thing not yet apprehended? On the other hand, if it is not understood by way of being pervaded by the mark (*liṅga*),

then if one were to postulate that inference has that [unapprehended] as its object, why could one not likewise postulate that smoke makes known the three worlds, since there is no difference in the absence of a relationship?
2.26 Now, as for the dependence of the manifestation of fire: if it is argued that the universal "fire-ness" (*agnitva-sāmānya*) is inferred by means of smoke through such dependence,
then is this dependence of the universal "fire-ness" determined by its being pervaded by smoke, or not?
If it has already been ascertained,
then inference does not escape the fault of apprehending what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhitva*).
If, on the other hand, it is argued that the dependence (*pāratantrya*) of the generality of fire upon smoke as its pervader has not yet been ascertained:
How it is inferred has been stated previously [at 2.3].
By this, the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of words such as "cow" has been exposed, because they merely convey things like the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) that were already perceived before.
How is that so?

What is being stated here: is it being propounded that the word "cow" (go-śabda) denotes the universal "cowness" (gotva) as it was understood at the time of grasping the convention, or does it denote an object distinct from that?

If it is proclaimed that the word "cow" makes known the very nature of cowness as apprehended at the time of grasping the convention, then the word "cow" does not attain the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it merely makes known an object whose form has already been cognized.

Now, if it is argued that even when the knower possesses the form of the object but lacks the capacity for cognition (*avedaka*), it still brings about validity (*prāmāṇya*), then the qualification "cognizing an object not previously apprehended" (*anadhigatārthagantṛ*) must have its scope specified.
Or, if [the qualification] means "denoting an object distinct from that [form],"...
At that time, the meaning would be understood from the word "cow" even without a conventional designation;
consequently, a contradiction with one's own established tenets would be unavoidable.
If it is argued that "cowness" itself is what is understood by the word "cow," [the response follows].
In that case as well, the reason for invalidity has already been elaborated: namely, the grasping of what has already been grasped (*gṛhītagrāhitva*).

If that [subsequent cognition] lacks validity, there is no establishment of the universal "cowness" (*gotva*). If that is not established, there can be no establishment of the locus through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

2.31 For this reason as well, the establishment of the locus through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is not tenable. Is the purpose of presumptive testimony to convey a locus already previously determined, or to convey a locus not previously determined? If presumptive testimony is restricted to a locus already previously determined, then it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it merely conveys an object that has already been established.

Furthermore, if it is the non-perception of the lump [of clay] that is the cause, then by the same logic of the impossibility of otherwise accounting for "cowness" (gotva), one would have to postulate the existence of elephants and horses as well.

If you argue that the present existence of what was previously determined is now ascertained through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), we ask: is this present existence distinct from what was previously determined, or is it non-distinct?
In that case, if it is non-different [from the Veda],
then how can those who know the Veda declare that presumption (*arthāpatti*) possesses authority as a means of knowledge, given that it merely communicates a meaning already determined previously?
Or, if it is a different thing, [how can it be authoritative]?
How is the universal "cowness" (gotva) cognized through the impossibility of its being otherwise?
It has been demonstrated more than once that if one accepts the cognition of that [universal], there would also have to be a cognition regarding elephants and horses.
This being the case, the statement that "present existence was not grasped by the previous cognition" is merely the prattle of a child.

2.4 By this, it should be understood that the validity of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is also refuted. 3.1 Likewise, for the followers of the Tathāgata as well, the qualification "cognizing an object not previously apprehended" is useless, because the possibility of excluding (or negating) such a cognition does not exist.
For two cognitions occurring at earlier and later times do not have a single object;
they do not have a single particular (svalakṣaṇa) as their object, nor do they have a single universal (sāmānya) as their object.
3.11 Because the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which possesses a single undifferentiated nature, is not distinct from the capacity to produce multiple cognitions occurring sequentially.
Furthermore, if it is argued that this is for the purpose of precluding the possibility of multiple cognitions arising simultaneously regarding a single object, that too is incorrect.
Otherwise, the cognitions of multiple persons arising with respect to a single object would result in being invalid.
(3.12) Now, if a qualification is employed for the purpose of excluding multiple cognitions that have a universal as their single object,
that too is incorrect.
There is no single cognition, nor is there a plurality of cognitions, because such [a plurality] is impossible in itself.
If there is an absence of that [object's] form, one must state the reason for the determination of each respective object—that consciousness has a universal as its object.
Alternatively, if that form exists, the universal would possess the nature of reality.
Or, if there were identity with a form that is not ultimately real, it would follow that the cognition itself is not ultimately real.
3.1a Furthermore, regarding two [cognitions] operating upon a single object, one must be either non-valid or lack the status of being a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
3.1a1 If it were non-valid, that would be untenable.
Since both [perception and conceptual cognition] consist in the apprehension of the same undifferentiated object, they must either both be valid or both be invalid, as no alternative is possible.
