If there were such an alternative, it would follow that there is a distinction between the cognitions of multiple persons produced regarding a single object.
Or else, [if one were to claim they are distinct], they would not be different types of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
That too is untenable.

Is it that the multiplicity of individual instances (*vyakti*) is not possible for the multiple cognitions—such as perceptions—produced from a single object, or is it the multiplicity of forms (*ākāra*) that is not possible?
If it is the case that the multiplicity of individual instances is not tenable, [then...]
That is incorrect, because we observe a plurality of individual instances in the various cognitions of multiple blue objects produced by a single blue object;
otherwise, the state of having multiple forms would not be possible.
That is incorrect, because we observe that cognitions of blue and light possess multiple aspects;
yet there exists no proliferation of blue (*nīla-prapañca*) that could produce them.
Because it is accepted by itself as having a single nature;
yet, if there were a single object, the designations "perception" and "inference" would be untenable.
This [objection] is incorrect.

This is because the designation [of the two cognitions] is justified by their being the effects of different instruments, just as the cognitions of Devadatta and others produced from a single blue object are designated as "the cognition of Devadatta" and so on due to being the effects of different agents; it is the same here as well.
Others, however, assert that valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is non-discrepant cognition.
What is this meaning of "non-contradiction" (*avisamvāda*)?

Is it (1) the apprehension of an object as it is established, or (2) being free from sublation (*bādhā*), or (3) being produced by the object that is being cognized, or (4) inciting activity toward the object that is being cognized, or (5) causing the attainment of the object?
3.21 If it is the apprehension of an object as it is established...
That is not tenable in the case of inferential cognition (anumānajñāna). 3.22 Now, if it is "being free from sublation" (bādhārahitatva), that too is not tenable in the case of inferential cognition.
3.23 Now, as for the claim that [the object] is produced by the implied meaning (*pratīyamānārtha*),
that too is not tenable in the case of inferential cognition (*anumānajñāna*),
because the universal form (*sāmānyākāra*) is excluded from being a producer.
Likewise, it is not tenable that even the experience of passion and so forth is produced by an appearing object,
because it lacks the capacity to produce itself.
Similarly, it is impossible for yogic perception to be produced by an object being perceived, because past and future things lack the capacity to act as causes.
If it were merely a producer [of activity], its status as past or future would be lost.
Alternatively, if being a motivator with respect to the perceived object constitutes non-contradiction, then even erroneous cognition possesses the quality of being a motivator.
A cognition of water arises based on a misconception, yet it lacks correspondence with reality;
even when a true cognition of water has arisen, one does not act upon it for some reason or other.
Even that would be non-concordant. 3.25 Now, if non-concordance consists in the attainment of the object,

does that mean the attainment of the mere object, or the attainment of the object as it appears, or the attainment of water of that same class, or the attainment of the object that produced itself, or the attainment of the causal factors that produced itself?
Is "non-contradiction" the state of being invariably realized?
If it means the capacity to lead one to the mere object itself,
then even the cognition of a mass of hair or two moons would result in being non-contradictory.

If, on the other hand, [validity] consists in the capacity to attain the object as it appears, then the non-contradiction of inferential cognition is not obtained, because it does not attain the object as it appears;
for in inferential cognition, it is the universal form that appears.
And that [object] is not attained by itself because it lacks existence.
Likewise, for the knowledge of a yogin that has arisen regarding a past or future object, there is no attainment of the object.
Similarly, even when the experience of passion and so forth has occurred, there is no attainment of the passion and so forth that appear [in that experience].
Likewise, even in the case of perceptual cognition, there is no attainment of an object that appears [in it], because it has already perished due to its momentariness.
If it is argued that non-contradiction consists in its leading to the attainment of water of that same kind,
that is incorrect, because the universal "water-ness" does not exist.
Now, if it is argued that the universal (jāti) is the exclusion of non-water-ness,
is that [exclusion] non-different from the individual instances of water or different from them?
If it is non-different, then it is merely the individual instance and not a universal.
Now, is that [non-existence] distinct [from existence], being either a real entity (*vastu*) or a non-entity (*avastu*)?
If it is a real entity, then there is an abandonment of what has been accepted.
If, on the other hand, it is a non-entity, how can there be a cognition of it?
Furthermore, a plurality of individual water-entities is not tenable;
how it is not tenable has been explained in the section on the definition of perception according to the Naiyāyikas.
Now, if non-contradiction (*avisaṃvādakatva*) is defined as the capacity to reach the object that produced it, [then...]
That is incorrect, because the eye, light, mental attention, and so forth have been refuted.
Alternatively, if "non-contradiction" means the necessary occurrence of the very causes that produce [the cognition] itself, [then it is not a valid definition].
Because in the absence of that [object], the absence of that [cognition] would follow as a logical consequence.
If this is so, then even the cognition of a mass of hair possesses non-contradiction by virtue of having a constant cause; otherwise, it would follow that it is accidental (*āka-smika*).
Such being the case, the statement that "one who acts after determining an object through these two [means of knowledge] is not contradicted in its causal efficacy" is merely the play of a child.
3.3 Likewise, even the enumeration of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*) is not tenable in the Buddhist view.
Why is that?
It is explained: there are only two means of valid cognition.
There is no other means of cognition [for it].
Is that duality [established] by a difference in individuals, a difference in forms, or a difference in objects?
3.31 If it is by a difference in individuals,
In that case, because individual instances of knowledge are infinite, they cannot be enumerated; furthermore, duality is untenable,
for there is no distinction among knowledges, since knowledge is distinguished from ignorance by its very nature as knowledge.
But how does it cease from another cognition?
Is it by way of being of the nature of cognition, or by way of another form?
If it were distinguished by being of the nature of cognition, [then...]
In that case, it would follow that other things are of the nature of ignorance, just like taste and so forth. Or,
if it is differentiated by another form,
then its being of the nature of ignorance arises, just like taste and so forth.
3.32 Now, if it is argued that there is a distinction between the two means of knowledge (*māna*) based on a difference in their forms (*ākāra*),
that too is untenable.
Apart from the form of cognition itself, there is no other form belonging to perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).
Or, if that [multiplicity] were admitted, there would be an absence of the form of cognition;
for cognition cannot consist of a collection of forms, since it is of a non-differentiated nature.
(3.33) Now, if it is argued that its twofold nature is established by means of the distinction between objects, [we reply:]...

3.331 Now, the object of inferential cognition must be stated: does it have as its object the particular (svalakṣaṇa) such as fire, or an existing universal (sāmānya), or an unreal universal, or is it without an object, or does it have its own [internal] aspect (svāṃśa) as its object?
If it has the particular such as fire as its object, [then...]

In that case, the distinction between perception and inference would be untenable, because their objects would be non-different. Alternatively, if it is argued that in inferential cognition only fire in general is apprehended, whereas in perception it is apprehended as having specific qualities such as being produced from grass and so forth; [then we reply:]...
If, in this way, inference does not transcend having the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object— assuming that it is merely the manifoldness (*prapañca*) of fire itself—
or if its object is the universal of existence (*satsāmānya*), [then...]
Nevertheless, there is no distinction between perception and inference, because the universal (*sāmānya*) has the nature of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, it is not possible for the existent universal to be an object of cognition, because, being eternal, it cannot logically function as a producer [of cognition] or as a donor of its form.
Nor can it be established that [cognition] is erroneous when it has the existent universal as its object.
Even if it is an error, it should not be said that it is a valid cognition (pramā) by virtue of its connection with a real object.
If, on the other hand, its object is a non-existent universal, then it cannot be an error, because that [universal] exists in its own form as a non-entity.
Furthermore, that which is non-existent cannot attain the status of being an object, because it lacks both the capacity to produce [cognition] and the capacity to impart its form [to cognition].
If it were not distinct from these two capacities, it would follow that it is a real entity (*vastu*). And if that were to follow, the distinction between perception and inference would be untenable.
If, on the other hand, it is without an object,
then there is no distinction between the two means of knowledge, because inferential cognition would lack an object.
Nor can there be error simply because of a lack of an object;
for neither error nor non-error is established for a cognition by its own mere existence,
but rather through the influence of external conditions.
Even if it were to have its own part as its object, there would still be no difference between perception and inference,
because both would have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object.
Furthermore, inferential cognition is not erroneous because it does not deceive regarding its own aspect (svāṃśa).
Likewise, the object of perception must also be stated: does it have as its object the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) such as form and so forth, or itself, or both?
If, in that case, it were merely an observer of form and so forth, [it would be erroneous].
That is incorrect, because if that [object] is not apprehended, there can be no apprehension of this [subject].
Furthermore, if it were to apprehend only the body of cognition,
that too is not tenable.
Because the status of being an object is established by its being a producer [of cognition] and its imparting a form [to it],
and neither production nor the imparting of a form is possible with respect to itself;
for something becomes an object only in relation to a subject.
Just as an effect depends upon a cause and a cause depends upon an effect, so it is here as well;
and if by means of perceptual cognition only the self is grasped as its own, then this same [dependence] exists in inference as well.
The distinction between perception and inference would be untenable. Furthermore, if it is argued that both are made objects of cognition,
that too is incorrect.
Because the apprehension of one [object] is established by the exclusion of the form of the second;
and if the apprehension of form were itself the apprehension of cognition, then form would possess the nature of cognition.
Either cognition itself possesses the nature of form, or the apprehension of form lacks the capacity to determine the form;
yet we do not observe two forms in a single [cognition].
3.3a Furthermore, the determination of duality is not possible here:
perception arises grasping itself as its object,
whereas inference does not take it as its object.
Likewise, inference also arises by assimilating itself [to its object],
and it does not illuminate perceptual cognition;
thus, the conventional usage of the number "two" would be untenable.
If it is argued that there is a determination of duality by means of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), that is incorrect;
for even that [conceptual construction], because it terminates in self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvedana*), does not grasp duality.
Alternatively, if it were apprehended, there would be the abandonment of what has been accepted;
and if that is untenable, to claim that "there are only two" is the behavior of a dull-witted person.
[Chapter 4: Examination of the Buddhist Definition of Perception]

4.1 Likewise, it should not be stated that "perception is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*)," because there is no possible object to be excluded (*apohya-artha*) for the term "free from conceptual construction.
[Objection: Is it not conceptual construction itself that is to be excluded?

[Response: What is this conceptual construction? Is conceptual construction a cognition produced by qualifiers such as qualities (*guṇa*), motion (*calana*), universals (*jāti*), and so forth; or is it that which produces recollection (*smṛti*)?

Is conceptual construction (kalpanā) consciousness; or is it the form of memory, or that which is produced by memory; or is it an appearance associated with verbal expression, or a cognition possessing verbal expression; or is it a conceptualization whose form is indistinct; or is it a mode of grasping an unreal object; or is it itself unreal; or is it the perception of an object from a three-featured logical mark (trirūpaliṅga); or is it an appearance of past or future objects?
4.11 Now, if cognition produced by qualifiers such as qualities (*guṇa*), motion (*calana*), genus (*jāti*), and so forth, is conceptual construction (*kalpanā*),

then is it a conceptual construction by virtue of being produced by qualifiers such as qualities, motion, genus, and so forth that are non-existent, or by virtue of being produced by those that are existent?
If its status as a conceptual construction is due to being produced by qualifiers such as qualities, motion, genus, and so forth that are non-existent, [then...]
That is incorrect, because that which does not exist lacks the capacity to be a producer, and thus cannot be an object of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).

If, on the other hand, it is argued that conceptual construction consists in being produced by qualifiers such as existing qualities, motion, or universals (*jāti*), then is this conceptual cognition possessed of an object (*saviṣaya*) or devoid of an object (*nirviṣaya*)?
Therefore, if conceptual cognition were to possess an object, that would be incorrect;

for even if it were produced by qualities, motion, universals, and so forth, it would not possess the nature of conceptualization, since it would not have transcended its arising through the power of the object itself.
Now, if conceptual construction (kalpanā) is that which is devoid of an object, then being objectless alone is the cause for its status as conceptual construction,
not the fact of being produced by qualifiers such as qualities, motion, or universals.
And if that [consciousness] were without an object, then it would be neither conceptual cognition nor non-conceptual cognition,
but would be mere consciousness.
If conceptualization were defined by its nature as cognition, then all cognition would be conceptual cognition.
(4.12) Alternatively, if conceptualization is cognition that produces memory, that is incorrect.

Memory also arises from the perception of form and so forth, yet it does not possess the nature of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), because of the statement: "When something has been seen in the presence of another, memory arises upon hearing the name of that [second thing].
(4.13) Now, if it is argued that memory is conceptual construction by virtue of its being of the nature of memory:

In that regard as well, is [conceptuality] defined by apprehending what has already been apprehended, by being devoid of an object, or by having the nature of apprehending an object not previously known?

If conceptuality consists in apprehending an object already apprehended, then even the first experience would result in being conceptual, since there is no difference in its apprehending an object already apprehended; this has been stated previously.
If [it is argued that it is non-conceptual] because it lacks an object,

then there is neither a conceptual form nor a non-conceptual form apart from the form of the cognition itself. Alternatively, if its status as conceptual is due to its grasping an object not previously apprehended, [then...]
That is incorrect;
for memory does not possess the quality of grasping an object not previously apprehended.
Due to the absence of that quality, it lacks the nature of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
If conceptualization consists in the apprehension of an object not previously perceived, then it would follow that cognitions of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth are conceptualizations.
Alternatively, if conceptualization consists in being produced by memory, [then the same consequence follows].
In that case, even the cognition of form and so forth, which is intended to be non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), possesses the quality of being produced by memory;
let it therefore be a conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*).
Alternatively, if it is not [produced by memory], then that conceptual cognition is produced by memory through its nature as awareness (*bodhasvabhāva*).
Conceptual cognition, however, arises in the form of recollection;
thus, this statement of yours—that [the object] is perceived by a mind oscillating due to my conceptualization—is devoid of logical justification.
For we do not observe two natures in a single entity.
4.15 Now, if conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is a cognition in which there appears a connection with verbal expression, then is that connection ultimate (*pāramārthika*) or non-ultimate?
If it is ultimate, [then...]
In that case, it would not possess the nature of conceptual construction (*kalpanātva*), just like the cognition of form and so forth.
If, on the other hand, it were not ultimately real, how could consciousness have its appearance [of a self], given the consequence that there is no self (*nairātmya*)?

Furthermore, no objective referent whatsoever is obtained in that which is unreal, because it is nothing other than the mere co-arising and existence of the capacity to produce [a cognition] and the imparting of its form.
And if it has the nature of apprehending an unreal object, then it is a mistaken cognition (*viparyaya-jñāna*).
And since that [definition] has been refuted by the term "non-erroneous" (*avyabhicārin*),
the term "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) need not be adopted.
4.16 Now, if conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is understood as cognition accompanied by verbal expression (*abhilāpa*),...
Is it of the nature of verbal expression, or is it produced by verbal expression, or is it the apprehension of verbal expression?
If it were of the nature of verbal expression, how could there be cognition?
If cognition consists of verbal expression, it should not be so stated,
because two contradictory forms cannot possess identity or coexistence. Or, if it is produced by verbal expression, [it is still untenable].
In that case, verbal cognitions would result in being conceptual;

and if they were conceptual, the linguistic determination of those [objects] would be untenable. Alternatively, if their status as conceptual is due to their being apprehended by means of verbal expression (*abhilāpa*), [then...]

In that case, all cognitions apprehending verbal expressions would fall under the category of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). If they were of the nature of conceptual construction, the establishment of linguistic conventions (*śabdavyavasthā*) would be untenable.
(4.17) Alternatively, if conceptual construction is defined as a cognition whose form is indistinct (*aspaṣṭākārā*), [then the following applies].
What is this lack of clarity (*aspaṣṭatā*)?

Is it the state of not having cognition as its essence, or being unproduced from a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), or being unproduced from the object being perceived, or the unreality of the perceived object, or the non-appearance of the particular characteristic?
If, first of all, lack of clarity consists in not having cognition as its essence, [then...]
That is incorrect;
for in this context, cognition is described as having an indistinct form— how could it possibly be non-cognitive in nature?

If, on the other hand, lack of clarity consists in not being produced from a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), then it follows that cognition would be accidental. If, however, it consists in not being produced from the object as it is perceived, [then...]
In that case, the perception of passion and so forth would become indistinct,
because it is impossible for passion and so forth to produce their own self-perception;
for it has never been observed before that entities can produce themselves.
Likewise, for the cognition of a mass of hair, there is no production of the mass of hair that is being perceived;
nevertheless, it arises with a clear appearance, and not with an unclear appearance.

Because of the statement that "for one bound by conceptual construction, there is no manifestation of a clear object. Now, if "lack of clarity" means the non-manifestation of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*),
then it follows that even the cognition of a mass of hair— which is considered non-conceptual— is lacking in clarity.
In that regard, because the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) does not appear therein, it is described as having a clear appearance; yet,
in the Tathāgata’s vision, there is no such knowledge that does not manifest the specific characteristic.
Because the body of knowledge (jñānakāya) appears within all cognition; if, on the other hand, indistinctness were due to the unreality of what is being perceived,
then it would follow that the cognition of a mass of hair or two moons is indistinct.

Nor is there unreality for that which is being perceived, because the collection of cognitions is itself being perceived; nor is there any contradiction in it. 4.18 Now, if conceptual construction (kalpanā) is defined as the grasping of an object that is not ultimately real, [then...]
In that case, even the cognition of a mass of hair would fall into the category of conceptual construction (kalpanā). Alternatively, if it is itself unreal,
how can there be a perception of it?

If it is argued that [the cognition] is a conceptual construction (kalpanā) consisting in the perception of an object through a mark (liṅga) possessing the three characteristics, then how could that cognition be non-ultimate (atāttvikī)? 4.1(10) If it is argued that... [it is a conceptual construction].
Is that [conceptualization] so designated because it is produced by a logical mark (*liṅga*), or because it lacks a real object?

If its status as conceptualization were due to being produced by a logical mark, then even non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-vijñāna*) which apprehends a logical mark would incur the status of being conceptualization.
Furthermore, there is no direct production of the cognition of the inferable object by the logical mark (*liṅga*).
If it is argued that [the cognition] is a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) because it lacks an objective referent (*nirviṣaya*), that too is not tenable.
Because inferential cognition has its own internal aspect as its object;
if there were no object distinct from this internal aspect,
it would be designated as a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) due to being devoid of an external object.
In that case, even the cognition of a mass of hair would fall under the category of conceptual construction (kalpanā).
Alternatively, if that which is non-conceptual arises with clarity, whereas inferential cognition appears indistinctly; [then there is a distinction].
Therefore, that [claim] that it is a conceptual cognition (kalpanājñāna) is incorrect;
furthermore, it is not possible for it to be indistinct (aspaṣṭatā).
This has already been stated previously [in verse 4.1(10)a2]:
"And what is the clarity of perceptual cognition?
Is it being produced by the particular (svalakṣaṇa), or is it the appearance of the particular?"
4.1(10)a21 Now, if it is produced from a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*),
is it produced from a particular characteristic that is being perceived, or is it produced from a particular characteristic contrary to that?
If it is produced from a particular characteristic that has ascended into cognition, [then...]
What appears in cognition? Is it the object, the cognition, or both? If it is the object, [then...]
That is incorrect, because when cognition is not itself perceived, that [object] does not appear. If, on the other hand, it is cognition [that is perceived],
then it does not produce itself, because an action cannot be directed toward oneself.
Now, if it appears that both [aspects] are present, that is incorrect,
because the apprehension of one [aspect] has as its inherent nature the exclusion of the form of the second.
And if both appear [simultaneously],
then it follows that cognition must produce cognition just as an object does;
and that is untenable because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself.
Now, if it is argued that [the universal] is not produced by the particular (svalakṣaṇa) because it is not perceived, then how can there be a cognition of it?
Precisely because it is not perceived, it cannot be known through direct perception (pratyakṣa).
Nor can it be established by inference,
because the logical marks of essential nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*) are not perceived.
There is no inference based on essential nature, for when there is identity with that effect, if that [identity] is not perceived, then that [nature] is not perceived.
Nor is there inference from an effect, because no effect produced by that [cause] is perceived;
for no effect produced by such things as a piśāca, atoms, or Maheśvara is observed here. If it is argued that knowledge itself is its mark (liṅga), [we reply:]...
That is incorrect, because no relationship between the two is perceived; it is merely consciousness itself, and not some other entity.
Furthermore, consciousness does not produce itself.
If it is argued that immediate cognition is its cause, that is incorrect, for there is no means of valid cognition for its apprehension.
Even that [cognition] which conceptualizes the object of another's mental continuum is not self-cognized by the cognition of its effect,
because it is distinct from it, just like the object of another's mental continuum;
nor is it [known] through inference.
Because its dependence on anything else is not perceived,
it penetrates itself as pure consciousness alone,
and not as dependent on another.
Because anything else would be equivalent to the Lord of Piśācas.

Furthermore, if clarity were due to being produced by an immediately preceding consciousness (*samanantaravijñāna*), then inferential knowledge (*anumānajñāna*) would also necessarily follow as being non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), since it too is produced by an immediately preceding cognition.
4.1(10)a22 Now, if clarity consists in the manifestation of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), then what manifests therein: is it the object, the cognition, or both?
If it is the object, [then...]
That is incorrect, because if establishment is not established, there is an absence of that establishment.
Alternatively, if it is cognition, [then...]
If that [object] also appears in inference,
let that too be non-conceptual.
If it is thus non-conceptual, then the object to be excluded by the term "devoid of conceptual construction" must now be sought.
Now, if it is argued that both appear, that is incorrect,
because it is accepted that the apprehension of one has the nature of existing by way of excluding the form of the second.
4.1(11) Now, if conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) has the nature of grasping objects that are past or future, what appears therein: the object itself, its absence, or nothing at all?
If the past object appears, [then...]
In that case, it would not possess the nature of a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), like the cognition of present blue;
nor would the object possess the state of being past, because it is being perceived, like blue water and so forth.
For there is no such thing as the "pastness" of that which is being perceived.
And if even that which is being perceived were said to be past, then everything characterized by cognition would become past;
consequently, there would be an absence of the conventional usage of the present.
Now, if its non-existence appears, even that has no pastness,
because it exists in its own form.

Nor is it tenable that the cognition having that as its object is conceptual, because it arises through the power of a non-existent thing; or, if there were no such power, the nature of the objective referent would have to be reconsidered. Or else, [the cognition] would be without an object.
In that case, that cognition of past and future objects is not described as being devoid of the assistance provided by past and future objects;

nor, while lacking an object, is it characterized as either conceptual (*savikalpaka*) or non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), but rather its status is established solely by virtue of its nature as cognition. Furthermore, its being conceptual is not intended on the basis of its being mere cognition alone, for that would entail the consequence that all cognitions are conceptual. If...
Furthermore, if the cognition of past and future objects is accepted as being conceptual because it lacks an external object,

then even the cognition of a mass of hair— which is intended to be non-conceptual— would necessarily be conceptual. Moreover, the cognition of the past and future cannot be devoid of an object, because it terminates within its own constituent parts (svāṃśa).
Nor is there any other object distinct from its own part, because it is excluded by the apprehension of a single [cognition].
Furthermore, deception regarding one's own part is not possible;
since that [deception] is absent, all cognition—whether conceptual or non-conceptual—must be declared as such, because a distinction [between them] is untenable.

4.1a As for what was also stated— that perception is free from conceptual construction because it arises through the power of the object, like the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form and so on— does this intend that it arises from the perceived specific characteristic, or rather that it arises from the mere object?
If it intends that it arises from the perceived specific characteristic, [then...]
In that case, it cannot be established that the perception of passion and so forth, as well as the yogic direct perception, arise from a presently perceived particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Alternatively, if this is stated as a proof— namely, "because they have arisen through the efficacy of an object" (*arthasāmarthyena samudbhūtatvāt*)— with the intention of referring to sensory direct perception,
even then [the argument fails], because that [proof] is intended to refute external objects.
Or let there be an external object;
even so, is it produced by that [object] as its efficient cause (*nimitta*), or as its material cause (*upādāna*)?
If it is produced by it as an efficient cause, [then...]
In that case, the form produced by that [form] would not attain the status of being a form, just like the cognition produced by a form that serves as its cause (*nimitta*).
Alternatively, if it is produced by that which consists of the material cause (*upādāna*),
then by this method the cognition attains the status of being a form, just like the form produced by a form.

Consequently, the entire world would consist of non-consciousness; and if the world were non-conscious, it would follow that the conventional usage of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*) would be impossible. And if that were to follow—
Of what is this characteristic being presented?
Now, if it is argued that form is produced by form as its material cause (*upādāna*), whereas cognition is produced by that which consists of the causal sign (*nimitta*):
This is the vision of one of great spiritual power; for no one who is not a fool would venture to speak thus,
for there is no such thing as a single entity possessing multiple forms.
Furthermore, by assigning multiple names, there is no difference in the object of cognition (*meyādyanyatva*) and so forth.

If there were such a difference, then one should not have said that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is produced by sensory consciousness (*indriyajñāna*) acting as a cooperative cause for the immediately succeeding object within its own domain.
Thus, in this way, sensory consciousness lacks the quality of arising from an object that is currently being perceived.
Furthermore, the example is devoid of the probans (*sādhanavikala*). For a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) such as form, there is no arising from an object that appears as form.

If, on the other hand, what I intend to express is "arising from a specific characteristic that is not being perceived," then it follows that non-conceptual cognitions—such as inferences regarding the past or the future—would become non-conceptual simply because they arise from objects that are not being perceived.
4.1b Furthermore, as for that which was stated: "By the power of the apprehension of one [thing], there arises from conceptualization the thought 'I perceive this' or 'I do not perceive that'";
for indeed, when there is the apprehension of a single ground, a conceptual cognition arises such as 'I perceive this' or 'I do not perceive that,' and so forth—this too is not tenable.

Just as the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form does not possess the capacity to produce conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-vijñāna*) because it is non-conceptual, so too the specific characteristic of consciousness does not transcend the state of not producing conceptual cognition, since there is no difference in their lack of discursive investigation (*avicāraka*).
Now, if it is argued that despite this lack of difference in non-discursiveness, non-conceptual cognition possesses the power to bring about the arising of conceptual cognition—
In that case, let this [absence of conceptual construction] also apply to the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form and so forth;
consequently, the distinction between perception and inference would be untenable.
Furthermore, as for what was stated otherwise—that the absence of conceptual construction in sensory cognition is established by perception itself—[this is not correct].
Now, what is this so-called "absence of conceptual construction"?
Does it refer to a body established as identical with the Knowledge-Body (*jñānakāya*), or one that is its opposite?
If it is established through identity with knowledge, [then...]
In that case, what is meant by "having perception as its means of establishment" and "being devoid of conceptual construction"?
It means that the form of cognition (*vijñānākāra*) is the means of establishing perception for the perceptual intellect;
it is not merely the absence of conceptual construction that is the means of establishing perception.
Inferential cognition (*anumāna-dhī*) is also established by means of perception (*pratyakṣa-sādhana*), because the form of the cognition exists even within the inferential cognition itself.
Now, if it is argued that even inferential cognition is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanā-rahitatva*) with respect to self-awareness (*ātma-saṃvitti*), [then...]
If it is argued that [cognition] consists of conceptual construction (kalpanā) in relation to external objects,
this confused statement pains the mind:
how could there be various forms for that single entity?
Now, if it is established as distinct [from cognition],
how can its apprehension occur?
It cannot be self-cognized, because it is distinct from the form of the cognition.
Nor is it apprehended by way of imparting a form that constitutes its cause, because absence lacks causal capacity.
This being the case, the claim that "the cognition of the sense-faculties is devoid of conceptual construction precisely because it is established by perception" is merely the prattle of a child.
Now, [if it is argued that] the cognition "this is a cow" and so forth is conceptual construction...

How is this [cognition] a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*)? Because it is not produced by the object: if an object such as a cow possessed the capacity to produce a cognition such as "cow," then it would do so even at the moment of the first contact with the sense organ, since its own nature remains unchanged. As it has been said:

That which was previously not a producer of cognition because there was no difference in its utility would likewise remain so later; therefore, even when the object has disappeared, visual cognition would still occur.

If, on the other hand, [the cognition] arises depending upon the recollection of the word, then let that [recollection] itself be the cause, because the cognition "cow" and so forth has its result immediately following that body [of recollection]. As it has been said:
"Even when there is contact with the object, the application of the word is again based on memory."
If sensory cognition were to depend [on that object], then that object would be obstructed.
This is incorrect;
even the initial cognition "it is a cow" is designated as the cognition "cow" when it is a consciousness that apprehends the individual substance of a cow.
Consequently, it also arises from the initial contact of the sense-organ with the object.
In this way, the two cognitions—the preceding and the succeeding—share a single object, such that both have the cognition "this is a cow" as their objective domain.
Now, does the capacity of a single entity to produce successive cognitions belong to it by means of one and the same nature, or by means of different natures?
We say that [the cause] produces [the effect] by means of a single nature alone.
But surely, if the preceding and succeeding cognitions were dependent upon a single nature, they would have to be simultaneous.

If this were so, then the cognitions of the eye and light produced by a single blue object would have to occupy the same location, possess the same form, and constitute a single individuality, because there is no distinction in their being produced from that same single blue object.
Now, its nature is such that it consists in the performance of various effects.

If this is so, then in my position as well, the nature [of the cause] consists precisely in the performance of multiple effects occurring in succession, because it arises as determined by the capacity of its own causes.
Alternatively, just as in your position, mental cognition has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object...
And it is not produced by the initial contact of the sense-organ; rather, it is generated by sensory cognition acting in conjunction with an object that immediately follows its own object.

Likewise, even cognitions such as "cow" are produced by a cognition born from the initial contact of the sense organ with its object, acting in conjunction with an immediately succeeding object of that same [sensory] domain, and being assisted by recollection and so forth; thus, there is no lack of an object, because another object— capable of generating the cognition "cow" and so on— arises in accordance with the capacity of its own causes.
Recollection, once arisen, is capable of producing the cognition "this is a cow.
This being the case, that which was stated— namely, "that which previously was not a producer of cognition," and so forth—
is merely chanted out without having considered either one's own or another's position.

4.1e Furthermore, there is no form of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) other than that which is distinct from the source of cognition (*jñāna*). For the form of conceptualization is established as being identical in nature with cognition.
Consequently, what is meant by saying that perception is "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*)?
Perception is that which is free from conceptual cognition (*jñāna*).
Whatever is tied to a specific intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), when that [nature] is withdrawn, it is withdrawn along with it.
Consequently, it follows that for the monks, perception would consist of ignorance (*ajñāna*).
Furthermore, even the term "non-deviant" (*avyabhicāri*) need not be included, because there is no possibility of a cognition to be excluded (*apohya*). [Objection:
But surely there exists a cognition produced by the collection of the sun's rays as its object; how can that be excluded?
Because its object is unreal water.
If its object is unreal water,
how can that [unreality] be removed, given that the form of unreal water exists in its own right, just like the forms of sweet water or long water?
Now, if sweet water exists there because it is perceived in its own form,
then here too water must be perceived, since we observe the conventional usage, "I perceive water; I am grasping water."
It is true that it appears so,
yet it appears as something unreal. What is this unreality?
Is it the non-existence of that which is being perceived, or is it that the perception itself is non-existent?
If it is the non-existence of that which is being perceived, then that [perception] does not appear here.
It appears precisely as the form of water.
Furthermore, that non-existence which is being perceived is itself untenable;
for when the form of an existent thing is being perceived, it is not logical to conceive of it as non-existent.

Otherwise, if the aspect of taste were being perceived, the aspect of form would have to be imagined; consequently, the world would remain unimpaired and undestroyed. Furthermore, if non-existence were appearing [as an object], [the world would likewise remain intact].
How can that cognition of water be called a false cognition (*mithyājñāna*), given that its object, the absence [of water], exists in its own form?
4.22 This cognition of water either takes water as its object, or the absence of water, or itself, or nothing at all.
4.221 If it takes water as its object, [then it is not false].
In that case, there is no falsity for him, just as in the case of the perception of sweet water;
for in that instance, real water appears.
Is that which appears real water?
Or rather, does that which appears to you seem real? If that which appears to you is real,
then here too water appears.
The reality of that [appearance] has also been established.
Now, as for that which appears as real, how is its reality known?
Is it by depending [on something] or otherwise?
If it is by depending, then here too a dependence arises.
Let it be that there is reality;
however, if reality is established independently of cognition, then things are well-established [in themselves].
All doctrines would be established. Now, if it is indeed perceived, yet it is sublated—
how strange it is that something is both perceived and sublated!
And being perceived is pervaded by the quality of producing [a cognition] and imparting its form;
and that which neither produces nor imparts a form does not appear, just as taste does not appear in the cognition of color. Yet, in this case, water is perceived.
The establishment of [the object's] being a producer and its imparting of form is possible; and when that is established, no sublation is possible,
because being a producer and imparting form is based upon existence.
4.222 Now, if it takes non-existence as its object, then it is not [a cognition] consisting of the nature of water-cognition, because its nature consists in the apprehension of non-existence.
Nor is it false, since it is logically established that it has non-existence as its object.

Furthermore, in the Buddhist doctrine, no object as a cause of cognition is possible in the case of a non-existent thing, because it lacks both the capacity to produce [cognition] and the capacity to impart its form. For the form of water is extracted from the cognition; yet foolish Buddhists attempt to establish the non-existence of that [form] here in relation to something that is not cognized.
Or, if [the cognition] has itself as its object, [then...]
Nevertheless, deviation is not possible, because it does not deceive its own part;
for cognition does not contradict itself.
Nor can it be designated as "water-cognition," just like the experience of passion and so forth;
for a cognition appearing blue is never observed to be designated as having the nature of a gustatory consciousness. 4.224 Or, if [it is argued that] it is objectless,
In that case, it is not actually a cognition of water,
yet it appears as a cognition of water;
therefore, we know that it is not without an object.
And if it were without an object, how could it be false cognition?
Based on the mere existence of cognition, there would be neither false cognition nor right cognition.
Furthermore, in your own position, cognition cannot be without an objective support (*nirālambana*), because it terminates within its own constituent parts (*svāṃśaparyavasitatvāt*).
4.23 Is the erroneous nature of consciousness due to conformity with its own existence alone, or due to conformity with the existence of another?
4.231 If it is due to conformity with its own existence, [then...]
In that case, all cognitions would become fallible, because the nature of being a cognition exists everywhere;
thus, no cognition whatsoever would be non-fallible. (4.232) Now, if it is argued that fallibility is asserted in accordance with the existence of another [external object],...
Is it by virtue of conforming to another existence that is non-beneficial, or by virtue of conforming to another existence that is beneficial?
If, by virtue of conforming to a non-beneficial other existence, there is variability,
then it follows that all cognitions would be variable, because there is no distinction among non-beneficial other existences.

Now, if it is argued that there is deviation (vyabhicāritā) due to the dependence on the existence of another entity that acts as an auxiliary, is this due to the dependence on the existence of another auxiliary functioning as an instrument (karaṇa), or rather due to the dependence on the existence of another auxiliary that has attained the status of an object (karman)?
If it is by way of the penetration of the existence of another auxiliary functioning as an instrument, [then...]
In that case, all cognitions would fall into falsity because of the existence of another entity that serves as the instrumental cause (karaṇa).
Alternatively, if falsity were due to the permeation by the existence of another entity serving as the object-cause (karmakāraka),
that too is untenable.
It is not false for that [cognition], because it is assisted by a causal factor (karmakāraka), just like the cognition of water that is real.
4.24 Likewise, what constitutes its being a correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*)? Is it by virtue of the mere existence of the cognition itself, or by virtue of the existence of another [object]?
4.241 If, therefore, correctness were to follow merely from the existence of cognition, then it would follow that all cognitions are correct, since the form of cognition is established in every case.
4.242 Alternatively, if correctness were to follow from the existence of another [object],...
In that case, is [the validity] due to conformity with another existence that provides no assistance, or is it due to conformity with another existence that does provide assistance?

If its correctness were due to conformity with another existence that provides no assistance, then it would follow that all cognitions are correct, because there is no distinction among other existences insofar as they provide no assistance.

Now, does this occur through the influence of the existence of another who is an auxiliary agent (*karaṇa*), that is, by the penetration of the existence of another who acts as an auxiliary agent; or rather, through the penetration of the existence of another who is an auxiliary object (*karman*)?

If it were through the penetration of the existence of another who is an auxiliary agent, then all cognitions would result in being valid (*samyaktva*), because there is no distinction in the existence of another who acts as an auxiliary agent.

Now, if correctness (*samyaktva*) is defined by the penetration of another existence that serves as an auxiliary factor for that which has attained the status of an object (*karmatāpanna*), then the experience of passion and so forth would not attain correctness,
nor would the cognition of a yogi regarding objects that are past or future.
4.25 Regarding that erroneous cognition,
is it produced by an erroneous apprehension of the material cause (*upādāna-jñāna*), or is it produced by a non-erroneous apprehension of the material cause?
4.251 If it is produced by an erroneous apprehension of the material cause, [then...]
Since that too is subject to deviation,
one encounters a succession of deviating factors; thus,
a non-deviating object to be apprehended cannot be found.
4.252 Now, if it is produced by the cognition of the material cause (*upādāna*), which is non-deviant, does that [cognition] arise by conforming to its material cause or without conforming to it?
If it is produced by conforming to the material cause,
What does it obtain then?
It is produced in conformity with the non-deviating nature [of the object].
How so? Because non-deviation is established through its identity with cognition.
Furthermore, there can be no imitation of a single part [of the object] by the material cause, because it is partless.
Consequently, it follows that all cognition would be non-erroneous,
and the cognition of an exclusion (apoha) would be impossible.
Furthermore, deviation and non-deviation do not exist as distinct from cognition;
just as the form of taste or the form of color is not different from the form of cognition,
so too deviation and non-deviation are not distinct from cognition.
And thus, the form of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is here refuted; what is being stated?
It is the form of cognition (*jñānākāra*) that is refuted here.
Consequently, it follows for the Buddhists (*saugata*) that perception (*pratyakṣa*) would be non-cognitive in nature (*ajñānātmaka*).
4.25 Furthermore, just as form is produced by form acting as its material cause (*upādāna*), so too is cognition produced by that which serves as its material cause;
for the very nature of that [cognition] is the production of form.
That same [cause] is also responsible for the production of his cognition;
for there is no difference in its nature as the producer of cognition.
If it is argued that [the cause] produces cognition by acting as the efficient condition (*nimitta*), while it produces form by acting as the material cause (*upādāna*), [we reply:]...

How, then, is it possible for a single entity to possess multiple forms? Furthermore, if there were a difference in designation, a difference in the object of cognition and so forth would not be possible;
it would follow that consciousness, like form, would possess the nature of form.
And upon attaining that [state], there is no self belonging to another world;
because of its absence, there is no other world.
Having placed this very point in his mind, the Blessed Bṛhaspati said: "Because of the non-existence of one who goes to another world, there is no other world."
Now, even if it is produced from matter as its material cause (*upādāna*), it would still be of the nature of cognition;
for matter too would then attain the nature of cognition because it is produced from matter as its material cause, just like cognition.
Or, if cognition is produced by cognition acting as its material cause, [then the same consequence follows].
Form is also produced by that very same [cause];
for there is no difference in its nature as the producer of form. And thus, entities possessing such or non-such natures are born from causes possessing such or non-such natures.
Is that [object], such as form and so forth, non-cognition, since it arises from causes not distinct from cognition?
Now, even though consciousness is produced from the appropriation of form (*rūpopādāna*), it does not have the nature of form;

likewise, even though consciousness is produced from the appropriation of cognition (*jñānopādāna*), it does not have the nature of cognition. Consequently, there follows the undesirable consequence of selflessness (*nairātmyaprasaṅga*).
Alternatively, if one imagines that consciousness has the form of cognition because it is produced from the appropriation of cognition, [then the same problem remains].

Likewise, if it were produced by the appropriation of form (*rūpa*), it would follow that it possesses the aspect of form; and if it were produced by the appropriation of light, it would possess the aspect of light.
Consequently, cognition would result in being composed of a collection of various aspects.
This is undesirable, however, because [cognition] is accepted as being non-dual in nature.
4.25b Regarding that consciousness which is produced by form: does it exist as being produced by form in one part, or is it established as being produced by form in its entirety?
If it exists in one part, [then...]
That is incorrect, because that which is partless cannot be devoid of a single part.
Alternatively, it would follow that [the object] is established as being produced in its entirety as a form.
In that case, consciousness cannot be produced [by a collection],

just as it is not observed that an effect— which is established as being produced by a single collection of causal factors— can be produced by a different collection. Consequently, the production of consciousness from a collection is untenable.
4.25c Likewise, form (rūpa) would also have to produce cognition either partially or by its entire self, resulting in the exhaustion of its capacity as an instrument.
If it produces it partially,
that is untenable;
Because that which is indivisible cannot have a single part [engaged in action].

If, on the other hand, it acts by means of its entire self, then form, having been exhausted in producing consciousness by means of its entire self, would not proceed toward the production of another form.
Just as a causal complex directed toward the production of a single effect does not produce another effect, so too form does not produce another form;
consequently, another form would be accidental.
If that [nature] were accidental, then the Buddhist inference from effect to cause would be destroyed.
Alternatively, if its essential form is established as being the producer of multiple effects,
then even such things as the number of a jar or a universal would likewise have a nature consisting of dependence upon multiple substrata.
The impossibility of the faults regarding the alternatives concerning subsistence.

(d.1) For this reason as well, the impossibility of the faults regarding the alternatives concerning subsistence [is established], because by means of the fault regarding the alternatives concerning subsistence, it is subsistence itself that is refuted,
not the jar, number, generality, and so forth.
Because they are distinct;
for there is no absence of one thing due to the absence of another, since there is no connection between them.
Indeed, when it is said that "the water-pot is without water," the absence of the water-pot itself is not understood.
It is not a matter of [the destruction of] the potsherds or that water;
rather, only the mere separation of the water from the water-pot is perceived.
But surely, the Naiyāyikas accept a general category of "pot" (ghaṭasāmānya) as possessing a subsistence?
In the absence of that [object], how could there be the persistence of it?
If this is so, then even for form, taste, and consciousness, the Naiyāyikas accept their occurrence, yet you [Buddhists] also accept their existence even in the absence of those [objects].
Now, if those [categories] appear even in the absence of a [real] function,
then they are accepted as such.
If this is so, then the nature of the pot, number, generality, and so forth also appears, by virtue of having an undifferentiated and pervasive essence.
Furthermore, the denial of that which is being experienced is not logical, as it would entail the absurd consequence of denying everything;
or, if it is not perceived, that very non-perception is sufficient [to establish its absence],
thus the fault regarding the alternatives of occurrence [of the cause] does not apply.
If it is perceived,
then the fault regarding the alternatives concerning its mode of existence (vṛtti) should not be stated; but if it is not perceived, [then the fault applies].
Nevertheless, it should not be said [that the universal is non-existent].
As for what was stated—that the universal of the jar (*ghaṭasāmānya*) is untenable because it is not perceived due to the difference in location—that too is incorrect;
for there is no difference in entities (*vastu*) by virtue of a difference in location.
Nevertheless, their own nature is experienced as being non-different and continuous through a distinction of form (*ākāra*).
It is not established that those two possess identity with their own substratum—the parts [of the whole]—merely because a spatial distinction is not perceived; nor is their non-existence established.
If there is perception by way of a distinction of form, [then they are distinct].
In that case, the non-apprehension [of difference] due to a difference in location is irrelevant as a reason,
because the difference in intrinsic nature has already been established by the apprehension of a difference in form.
Or, if there is no cognition of it as having a different form, [then the object is not perceived].
Let that [non-existence] itself be so, because it is capable of functioning as the conventional usage of "non-existent.
What is the use of postulating the non-apprehension of a difference in location?
Since it arises from its own causes as restricted by specific place and time, there is no apprehension of it in another location or at another time.
Otherwise, there would be a non-existence of form and so forth, because that which is contiguous with another location would not be perceived.
As for what was also said— that the universal "jar" does not exist because it is not perceived when [the jar] is not perceived— what is established by this?
Is this intended to demonstrate the non-difference [of the whole] from its parts as the locus, or to demonstrate its non-existence?
If it is a demonstration of non-difference that is being made, then what is the subject (pakṣa) here?
Is it the generality of the pot (*ghaṭasāmānya*) that is the subject, or rather that which resides in its parts?
If it is the generality of the pot that is being proposed as the subject (*pakṣa*),
is that [generality] already cognized or not yet cognized?
If that [reason] belongs to one who has not understood [the subject],
that is incorrect;
for there is no arising of a reason when the locus (dharmin) is not understood.
Nor is there the capacity to convey [the meaning] when the basis is deficient.
If, on the other hand, it is that which is already understood, then by that very apprehension of a distinct form, the means of proof that conveys non-difference is sublated.
Now, if that which has those parts as its substratum is made the subject (*pakṣa*), even there one must ask: is non-distinction from its own nature (*svarūpa*) to be proven, or from another?
If non-distinction from its own nature is what is being proven, [then...]
They should be addressed as having already established what is to be proven.
Now, if non-difference from another is being proven, is that other self already understood or not understood?
If it has been apprehended, is it apprehended as having a distinct form or as having a non-distinct form?
If it is perceived as having a distinct form, [then...]
In that case, by this very apprehension of distinct forms, the means of proof that establishes non-difference is sublated.
Alternatively, if it is apprehended as having a non-distinct form, then it is not another self.
Now, since non-distinction from one's own essential nature is what is to be proven, they must be addressed as proving what is already established.
Alternatively, if it is not understood [as such],
then there is no unity, just like that between a chariot and a horse's horn.
Now, if non-existence is the probandum, in that case too, what is being made the subject (*pakṣa*)?
Is it the generality of the jar, or rather its locus consisting of its parts?
In that case, if the generality of the pot (ghaṭasāmānya) is made the subject of the argument,
is it one that is already cognized or one that is not cognized?
If it is one that is already cognized, [then...]
In that case, because the reason for non-existence is sublated by that very same apprehension of existence, it lacks probative force (*agamakatva*).
Alternatively, if it is not apprehended,
how can it be made the subject of the thesis (*pakṣīkaraṇa*), since it is impossible to make something itself unapprehended the subject of the thesis?

Now, regarding the formal argument (*adhikaraṇa*) concerning parts: the thesis is that "there is no such thing as the universal *ghaṭa*," and for the reason "because it is not apprehended when those [parts] are not apprehended," there is no connection with its non-existence.

Since the relations of identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*) are absent, how can there be any power of proof (*gamakatva*)? What is the meaning of the phrase "because it is not apprehended when those are not apprehended"? Is it...?

Is it intended that the apprehension of the substratum consisting of the parts is itself the apprehension of the jar-universal; or is it the apprehension of the jar-universal subsequent to the apprehension of the substratum consisting of the parts; or rather, is it intended that there is no apprehension of the jar-universal at all? If, first, it is intended that the apprehension of the substratum consisting of the parts is itself the apprehension of the jar-universal, [then...]
In that case, neither non-distinction nor the non-existence of either one is established by this [argument].
Just as, even when blue and its cognition are perceived together, there is neither the absence of one nor their non-distinction,
so too, even when blue and red are perceived together, there is neither the absence of one nor their non-distinction.
Now, if what is intended is that the apprehension of the pot as a generality (*ghaṭasāmānya*) follows immediately after the apprehension of its parts (*avayava*),
then by this [fact] neither non-difference nor the non-existence of one of the two is established.
Just as the perception of taste following the apprehension of color does not lead to the conclusion that those two are identical, nor that one of them is non-existent.

If, on the other hand, the non-apprehension of the universal "jar" itself is what you intend to express, then you should not say "because it is not apprehended when that [the jar] is not apprehended"; let there simply be "because of non-apprehension.
Not so.

For the non-perception of one thing is established only when another is not perceived, because that non-perception is based on the exclusion of its own nature [from that other]. Furthermore, the meaning of "exclusion" (*vyatireka*)—namely, that "because it is not perceived when that [other] is not perceived"—is not obtained here; for there is simply no perception of the generality (*sāmānya*) of the jar.
Rather, what is obtained is the perception of the generality of the jar immediately after the perception of the locus consisting of its parts.
And consequently, because it proves the opposite, it is contradictory (*viruddha*).

As for what was further stated— that there is no universal (*sāmānya*) because of the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions of perceptibility at the time of perceiving a single individual mass—
who says that the universal is not perceived?
Rather, it is indeed perceived.
How is this known?
Because when a second or subsequent individual is seen, there is the observation of memory regarding the preceding individual.
He recollects it as being similar to this.
Alternatively, at the time of grasping a single mass, that [object] does not possess the characteristics for perception; therefore, it is not perceived.
Here, "possessing the characteristics for perception" means the occurrence of a collection of multiple auxiliary factors.
And if it has reached the conditions for perception,
how is it not perceived?
Or, if it is not perceived, [then...]
In that case, it has not reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).
Here, reaching the conditions for perception consists in the completeness of other causal factors (*pratyayāntara*) and a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*).
If these exist, how can there be non-perception?
If non-apprehension is postulated even for such a [thing], it follows that all entities would be non-apprehended;
or, if they are apprehended, another cause must be sought.
Alternatively, if what is intended is merely the completeness of other conditions, [then...]
That is not a specific property of its own nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*).
If this were so, there would be non-perception only of the imperceptible, and no non-perception of the perceptible. If...
Furthermore, if the completeness of other causal factors is defined as reaching the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*),
then there must be perception and not non-perception;
for the completeness of the other causal factors is the capacity to produce perception.
If that [object] exists, how can there be non-perception?
Therefore, it is only for that which has reached the conditions for perception (*anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*) that there is non-perception.
[This refers to] that which has reached the condition of being unperceivable.
Furthermore, as for what was said—that there is no universal (sāmānya) because it is not perceived separately [from individuals], like milk and water—that too is incorrect.
For "separateness" (viveka) is indeed the difference in form among individuals, their lack of a common nature.
The universal, however, is the recurring form—the similarity between these two and their similarity with those others—because we observe the perception of distinct forms.
Likewise, even in the case of milk and water, there is indeed a distinct apprehension;
for instance, when milk and water are placed together in a single vessel, [their distinction remains perceptible].
Does only milk appear, or water, or both?
If it is milk alone that appears, how is it not distinct from the form of water?
Now, if only water appears,
how is it that even this is not distinct from the milk? Or, if both appear, [how is it so]?
Therefore, there is the apprehension of both as mutually distinct from one another's form, because they are excluded from identity.
(d. 6) Furthermore, as for what was said elsewhere: "A difference observed in one place is not seen anywhere else;
therefore, there is no other universal distinct [from the particular], because cognition is non-different."
This too is incorrect;
for there certainly is the perception elsewhere of a distinction observed in one place,
just as there is the apprehension of a jar, a cloth, or the like when it is seen upon one part and remains attached to another part.
Likewise, the universal (sāmānya) is also distinct, because it is determined through the difference in cognitions that possess a recurring form.

Furthermore, as for the other point stated— that the universal is non-existent because a permanent entity lacks the capacity to perform causal efficiency either successively or simultaneously— that is incorrect.
In both cases, the accomplishment of purposeful action is possible, whether simultaneously or sequentially.
But surely, sequential agency is not possible for that which is non-different [from itself]; it would follow that all effects occur at one and the same time.
And this is incorrect:

just as in your own position, a single blue particular (nīla-svalakṣaṇa) produces effects of multiple forms—such as the visual organ, light, and mental attention—which are restricted to specific locations;
yet, even though these effects arise from a single nature, they do not possess a single form or a connection to a single location.
Likewise here too, it is of such a nature:
that universal (*sāmānya*) consists in the production of effects either successively or simultaneously.
Now, if it produces an effect successively, [how can it be a single entity?]
Then that very same thing would be both the producer and the non-producer.
True; that very same thing is both the producer and the non-producer. But surely this entails the consequence of a distinction between the producer and the non-producer?
There is no such consequence;
for according to your own position, a single blue particular (nīla-svalakṣaṇa) is a producer with respect to its own effect, yet it is a non-producer with respect to its own cause-nature.
There is no difference in its own nature; furthermore,
it is illogical that it should produce both its own cause and itself.
Therefore, that which acts as a self must act either upon what has already arisen or upon what has not yet arisen.
If it acts upon what has already arisen, that is illogical.
Because it is impossible to produce what has already been produced; and if one produces what has not yet arisen, what is the meaning of an agent for that which is non-existent?
Likewise, it does not produce its own cause either, because that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence.
Therefore, that very same thing is both an agent and a non-agent; likewise, a universal is both productive and non-productive.
Furthermore, the absence of causal efficiency (arthakriyā) does not establish non-existence.
Just as the nature of fire does not cease even when it lacks the capacity to produce smoke during its state as a red-hot iron ball or charcoal.
Because it arises from its own cause as being of such a nature— namely, having the nature of fire yet being of a nature that does not produce smoke—
and likewise because other effects are also produced by their own causes as being real entities (vastu-svabhāva) yet of a nature that does not produce those specific effects;
so too, the universal, though being a real entity, does not produce an effect.
But if it does not produce an effect,
how do you know that it exists? By its apprehension.
Now, one might ask: how can there be a cognition of that [object] if it is not produced by it?

[The answer is: because it arises as having the nature of a cognition of that [object], being determined by the capacity of its own causes. Nor is the status of being a cognition of that [object] due to being produced by it.
Otherwise, it would follow that even the eye and other sense organs are objects of cognition.

Nor can the status of being a grasper of an object be established by its possessing the form of the object, because it is impossible for the form of the object to enter into [the consciousness] apart from the nature of consciousness itself.
As for this form which is imparted by the object—
Is that [object] different from the form of cognition or non-different?
If it is different,
is it real or unreal?
If it is real,
how is its cognition [established]? Is it by way of being self-cognized, or rather by way of being a producer or an impartor of form?
If it is [established] by way of self-cognition,
that is incorrect, because since it does not have consciousness as its nature, self-cognition is impossible.
If [the object] is [known] by way of imparting its form as that which possesses the nature of being a producer, then an infinite regress of forms would result;
but if it is not real, [then...]
That [subject-object] relation is not tenable, because it would entail the absence of both self-cognizability and the nature of being a producer.
Alternatively, if they are non-distinct,
is that [relation] real or unreal?
If it were real, would it be insentient by nature or the opposite?
If it were insentient by nature, [then...]
In that case, there is no identity with consciousness;
for the identity of the conscious and the unconscious is untenable. Or, if it were the opposite [of that],...
In that case, there would be mere cognition;
and since the nature of cognition is common to all cognitions, the specific determination of each respective object would be untenable.
Now, if [the form] were unreal (atāttvika),...
In that case, even cognition would result in being non-real.
Furthermore, if the arising of an aspect occurs through identity with cognition, then cognition—
Since it is produced by all causal factors, it would be common to all [cognitions], and thus the determination of each specific object would be untenable.
This being the case, what was stated— that "it connects this [cognition] with the object, for it does so without abandoning the form of the object"— is undermined.
Therefore, the conformity to the form of the object of cognition is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the apprehension of that object.
That is the deluded play of the Buddhists.

(d. 8) Thus, the refutation regarding the alternatives of subsistence and so forth does not apply to the universal and the like; for just as a single form is common by virtue of producing multiple effects, so too a single universal is common to multiple substrates.
Now, does a single form not produce multiple effects,
but rather only one?
In that case as well, does it produce only another form, or only cognition?
If it produces form alone,
then the non-perception of form would follow because consciousness is not produced;
or if it produces consciousness alone, [the same fault follows].
Nevertheless, mental perception is not attained [by that definition].
That which is produced by sensory cognition, acting as a cooperative cause with an object immediately following its own object, is mental perception.

Furthermore, there is no object that exists immediately after its own [perceiving] object, because it does not produce another form. Therefore, one must understand that there is only a single form which is common to the effects such as consciousness and blue.
Do the causes—eye, form, light, and so forth—which produce consciousness, possess a single nature, or do they possess distinct, determined natures?
If, therefore, they produce [the effect] by way of having a single nature, then the identity of the agents follows, because of their connection with an undifferentiated nature.
Or, if they— possessing restricted natures— generate an effect in the form of cognition, [then...]

In that case, the non-differentiated nature of consciousness would cease to exist, because it would be produced by causes possessing restricted natures, just like [the perceptions of] form, sound, and so forth. Alternatively, if an undivided effect were to arise even from diverse causes,
then— in such a case— the inference of distinct causes based on the difference of effects would be precluded.
Even from a single-natured consciousness, multiple effects such as the eye, light, and so forth arise;
likewise, even from multiple [causes], a single [effect] comes to be.
This being the case, the inference of a specific cause based on the observation of a specific effect is undermined.
Now, if a single effect arises from only a single cause, and not from many causes combined to produce a single result,
then by what means can one refute the inference of a specific cause upon the observation of a specific effect?
This [position] is incorrect.

If a single cause produces a single effect, then there is a contradiction with your own tenet that "from four [causes] arise mind and mental factors," and that "from cognition comes the nature of being cognizant, and from the object comes the form of the object," and so forth.
Does it produce only one [effect],
or rather [many] by virtue of their belonging to the same genus?
Is it by virtue of having that same form, or by virtue of occurring at earlier and later times? If its status as a producer were due to being of the same class,
then it would produce even that which arises later, provided it is of the same class.
If it is the producer by virtue of conforming to that form,
then this same refutation applies there as well.
If, on the other hand, it is the producer by virtue of existing at earlier and later times, [then...]

In that case, it should not be said that the eye alone is the producer, since there is no distinction among the eye, visible form, light, and mental attention in terms of their existence at a prior time.
Furthermore, by being produced from multiple causes, consciousness would result in having the nature of a mere collection of non-agents.
Or, if the forms of visible form and so forth were excluded, the form of consciousness itself would be untenable.
If that were untenable, it would follow that there is no self (nairātmya).
Furthermore, is cognition (jñāna) of the nature solely of an effect, solely of a cause, or of both?
If it were of the nature solely of a cause, [it would be eternal].
In that case, the nature of being an effect is not possible;
and in the absence of that, there is no substantiality, because it is accepted that conditioned phenomena possess substantiality.
Nor is the nature of being a cause tenable, because since no excellence (*atiśaya*) is imparted [to them], they lack the capacity to produce [an effect].
Even if it has the nature of having only its effect as its essence,
it still does not consist of existence,
because it lacks the status of a real entity (*vastutva*) in the performance of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
Now, that which is of a dual nature becomes both one and manifold; by whom have you been deceived?
For multiplicity is not established by assigning multiple names to a single entity;
nor is the assignment of multiple names tenable, because the causal basis (*nimitta*) is not manifold.
Thus, when consciousness is impossible, the continuity of the stream (*santāna*) is untenable, as is the duality of the non-erroneous and the erroneous.
