e.1 For this reason as well, the continuity [of consciousness] is not established, because consciousness is unitary.
And that unity [is maintained] because the occurrence of another aspect is impossible;
or, if such an occurrence were possible, it would entail the consequence that cognition is devoid of aspects.
And if that were the case, the continuity of the stream would be untenable.

For this reason as well, the continuity of consciousness is untenable: if consciousness ceases from a non-existent state to become an existent self-nature, how could it then turn away from that very nature to become something else?
Is it by way of its being the nature of existence, or by some other mode?
If it were to be excluded by way of its being the nature of existence, then form and the rest would result in having the mode of non-existence, just like the horns of a horse.

If, on the other hand, it ceases by way of another mode, then cognition would result in having a non-existent nature, like a horse's horn. Now, if cognition ceases from form and so forth by way of being a mode of consciousness—that nature of consciousness as a mode of consciousness is either existent by nature or non-existent by nature. If it is existent by nature, [then...]
In that case, what is meant by the statement that [the object] ceases by way of being a form of cognition?
It would mean that it ceases by way of having existence as its nature, because there is no distinction between consciousness and the form of existence.
Consequently, it follows that form and so forth would possess the character of non-existence, like a horse's horn; thus, the very same refutation previously mentioned is incurred.
If, on the other hand, it has a non-existent nature,
then like a donkey's horn, it would abandon its character as consciousness;
and if that character were abandoned, the continuity of the stream of consciousness would be impossible.
And if that [continuity] were untenable, then rituals such as the veneration of a *caitya* would be purposeless.

For this reason as well, the continuity of consciousness (*vijñānasantāna*) is untenable: because the consciousness that produces [a subsequent moment] possesses no distinction in its essential nature (*svarūpa*) with respect to the preceding, the subsequent, or the simultaneously arisen consciousness.

That which is the essential nature of a consciousness in relation to a preceding or simultaneous consciousness is the very same essential nature in relation to a subsequent consciousness, since consciousness is partless (*niravayava*).

Consequently, just as it is not the cause of the preceding co-arisen cognition, so too it is not the cause of the subsequent cognition, because no additional operation distinct from its own nature is perceived.
If, on the other hand, it is argued that its status as a cause is established by means of an excellence (atiśaya) existing at the prior time;

If this were so, then just as Devadatta’s cognition existing at a time prior to [another] cognition of Devadatta is the cause of that cognition of Devadatta, it would follow that Devadatta’s cognition is the cause of all cognitions of persons produced at times prior to Devadatta’s cognition.
If that were to follow, there would result the recollection of objects experienced by persons separated by many islands and regions.
Likewise, there would be recollection even of objects never experienced, such as one's own kinsmen or snakes.
Furthermore, if the cognitions of Devadatta and others were produced by the pure knowledge of a Tathāgata, those cognitions would themselves be pure;
consequently, everyone would be omniscient.

Furthermore, the cognitions of Devadatta and others would not possess purity, because even though they are produced from the material cause of the Tathāgata’s pure cognition, they are also produced by the cognitions of Devadatta and others.
If [the Tathāgata’s cognition] were to attain its pure form merely by being produced from that [pure cause],
then it would follow that he too would be one who has not abandoned passion and would not be omniscient.
Furthermore, a continuum is untenable if two consciousnesses arise simultaneously, because the relationship of cause and effect is impossible [in that case].
For your established tenet is that at the very moment the causal consciousness perishes, the resultant consciousness arises.
Furthermore, the destruction of the cognition of the cause occurs simultaneously with its arising.
Consequently, at the time when the cognition of the cause is destroyed, the cognition of the effect comes into being; what does this mean?
It means that it comes into being at the very same time as the cognition of the cause arises.
Furthermore, it is impossible for there to be a cause-and-effect relationship between two things that arise simultaneously, just like the horns of a cow that emerge at the same time.
Moreover, just as an unarisen causal cognition would have to arise, it would follow that it must also perish while unarisen;
consequently, it would not be perceived even for a single moment.

Alternatively, if there were perception [of it], there would be the consequence of its being perceived continuously, because that destruction which is identical with its nature cannot act as an obstacle to perception.
If it were to act as an obstacle, there would be the consequence that even the perception of a single moment would be impossible.
Now, if it has arisen with a nature that is perceivable for only a single moment, then there is neither continuous perception nor non-perception.
If this is so, why is it not postulated that [the entity] has arisen with a nature perceivable in twelve or eight moments?
Furthermore, if there is no difference between arising and destruction, would there not be a simultaneous destruction of both cause and effect?
It might be argued:

"Furthermore, it has been stated that the initial cognition immediately following emergence from the mother's womb is preceded by another cognition, because it is a cognition, like a second cognition.
This is not so, because the example is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Furthermore, it has already been explained that even for a second or subsequent cognition, its being preceded by a [prior] cognition cannot be apprehended.
Moreover, if one were to infer that a cognition is preceded by another cognition simply because it is a cognition, [the following would apply].
Indeed, it is said that an effect characterized by cognition cannot arise without a cause characterized by cognition;
yet this is a flaw,
for [cognition] also arises from causes such as blue objects, light, and the eye, which are not themselves of the nature of cognition.
Likewise, the initial consciousness at the beginning of conception and so forth will arise from the very aggregate of the elements alone; another preceding consciousness need not be postulated.
That which arises immediately after something else is the cause of that [latter],
not one whose capacity is unobserved.
In the absence of consciousness (*vijñāna*), the state of having a form produced by consciousness ceases,
but not the state of having a form of cognition (*jñāna*).
This is just as, when mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises without the operation of the sense organs, it lacks the form produced by the sense organs.
[The object] ceases, but not its nature as a form of cognition.
And if the production of a similar [effect] from a similar [cause] were strictly determined, then by means of smoke...
Inference of fire would not be possible,
because it is impossible for fire to be the material cause [of smoke] without similarity to smoke.
If it is argued that "similarity" refers to the two having the same nature (rūpa-rūpatā), [we reply:]...
Therefore, in this case as well, the similarity between the primary elements and consciousness consists in their having the nature of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*);
enough with the postulation of a consciousness belonging to another world.
If it is argued that since the primary elements do not possess the nature of consciousness, they cannot be the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) of consciousness;
In this case as well, the nature of smoke does not exist in fire, nor is it its material cause;
in the absence of that, there can be no inference of fire.

Likewise, from the cognition of an experience, only the cognition of that experience itself must be admitted to arise, because it is accepted that an effect arises by conforming to its material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).
Nor is there conformity with only a single part [of the object], because that seed [of the cognition] is not variegated.
Furthermore, if it did not conform to the form of the experience, it would lack the very nature of being a cognition.

And since it imitates the nature of consciousness, how could it not be of the nature of experience? If that were established, an infinite regress of experiences would result; thus, memory would be impossible. And if that [memory] is impossible...
Furthermore, inferential cognition would also be untenable;
consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total collapse of all worldly conventions.
And thus, the establishment of a continuum would not be possible.
Furthermore, in the Buddhist system, there is no duality of cognition consisting of conceptual and non-conceptual knowledge, nor is a twofold division into errant and non-errant cognition tenable.
[Chapter 5: Examination of Mīmāṃsāsūtra 1.1.4]
5. Likewise, that which is stated—"the arising of cognition when a person's sense organs are in contact with existing objects is perception"—that too has been refuted.

How so? This sūtra is sometimes intended as a definition (*lakṣaṇa*), sometimes intended to set forth the number of grammatical factors (*kāraka-saṅkhyā*), and sometimes intended as a restatement (*anuvāda*). 5.1(1) If it is intended as a definition:

At that time, the non-erroneousness of the cognition cannot be apprehended—neither by virtue of being produced by unimpaired causes, nor by the efficacy of purposeful action, nor by the absence of sublation, nor in any other way.

All this should be stated by recollecting what was previously said. Furthermore, the fact that a cognition arises from the contact of a sense organ with its object is not perceived by one who perceives only the proximate part [of the object], because that contact is supersensible (*atīndriya*) and is therefore not apprehended at that time.

Nor can it be understood that [cognition] is produced by the sense organs, precisely because the sense organs themselves are beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*). If it is argued that the postulation of sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) is made because cognition would otherwise be inexplicable, such inexplicability of cognition does not exist. What inference [could there be]?
5.2 Now, if it is for the sake of defining the number of factors (kāraka), what is the purpose of that enumeration?
Since light and so forth are also factors, they too would have to be enumerated.
5.3 Now, as for the status of being a restatement (*anuvāda*):
a restatement concerns what is already established, not what is unestablished; and perception is not known to exist anywhere [as a means of knowing the self].
Is it not known in common experience?
We say it is not known because it is not apprehended with certainty;
nor is its being produced from the contact of a real object known.
Consequently, there would be no apprehension through perception; and if that is not apprehended, a restatement (anuvāda) is untenable.
For this reason as well, a restatement is untenable due to the absence of purpose.

For a restatement does not proceed without a purpose; having restated something, one prescribes or prohibits something in a particular instance. But surely, even here, the status of being a cause with respect to dharma is prohibited.
Thus it has been said: with respect to *dharma*, perception is signless (*animitta*) because it apprehends what is present and because it arises from sensory contact.

In this regard, is it being denied that perception—arising as a manifestation of an object other than *dharma*—serves as a cause for *dharma*, or is it perception arising as a manifestation of *dharma* itself, or perhaps one that has not yet arisen?
If, then, the exclusion of perception arising as a manifestation of an object other than *dharma* is being made...
Then those of dull intellect should be enlightened by means of non-contradiction.
However, if a refutation is made through the exclusion of perception that has arisen from the awakening to the Dharma, then one stands opposed by way of contradiction.
It is contradictory to assert that direct perception (pratyakṣa) arises as a cognizer of phenomena (dharma) and yet is not caused by the signs of phenomena (dharmanimitta).
Otherwise, even the cognition produced by speech or silence would—by virtue of arising as a cognizer of phenomena—not have those [speech and silence] as its cause.
If, on the other hand, it is argued that what has not arisen cannot be a cognizer of phenomena, [then the same applies to direct perception].
By what means is it established here that which has not arisen is a cognizer of phenomena?
Nor is it a cognizer of the lotus petal, because it itself does not exist.
As for what was also said—that [perception] arises from contact with an existing object—[that too is untenable].
That too is incorrect; how it is not the case that [perception] arises from contact with an existing object has already been explained previously (5.3b).
Furthermore, as for what was stated otherwise—that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is indeed a cognition that apprehends what is present because it perceives only what exists—[that is also untenable].
If this is so, then not only perception,

but rather every cognition produced by all means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is a cognizer of what exists; whereas cognition generated by [mere] instruction is a cognizer of an object that is to be accomplished but does not yet exist.
If it does not exist,
how can it be understood? Or, if it is understood, [how can it be non-existent]?
How is it that [the object] does not exist?

Existence occurs precisely through the fact of being cognized, just like an object cognized by the means of valid perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, cognition does not arise without an object to be cognized, as in the case of perceptual cognition.

Moreover, the falsity of the consciousness produced by the words of an injunction (*codanā*) is established because its object is non-existent, just like the cognition of a mass of hair [in one suffering from ophthalmia].
Even the cognition of a mass of hair is false when there is an absence of an object that provides the perceived assistance;
likewise here, since the object providing the perceived assistance does not exist at all,
how can it not be false?
Alternatively, in that lineage [of interpretation], the capacity of the word of injunction (*codanā*) to have as its object a thing to be performed (*kartavya*) would be lost.
Furthermore, does the cognition produced by an injunction have as its object a thing to be performed, or does it have as its object the absence of such a thing, or is it without an object?
If it has as its object a thing to be performed, [then...]
In that case, its very state of being present [is established], because it is manifested through cognition, like water and so forth that are currently existing.
The non-cognition of water and so forth occurs by means of such causes as their own existence or their status as producers when fire is present, as indicated by smoke.
And if this [non-cognition] exists, [then the object is not present].
How is there non-existence?
If it has the absence of that [object] as its object, then since even that [absence] exists by way of its own nature, it cannot be something to be produced.
If, on the other hand, it is without an object,
then it cannot be said that the injunction makes known what is to be done;
rather, one must say that it is simply without an object.

This being the case, just as perception is the apprehender of what is present, so too are the other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Perception is the arising of cognition, and there is no further means of valid cognition for the apprehension of that cognition.
It is not apprehended through direct perception, because it is not itself admitted [as such].
Nor is it accessible through inference, because no probans (liṅga) invariably concomitant with it is perceived.
Now, suppose it is cognized through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).

Is it because the purpose of the jar is otherwise inexplicable, or because the acquisition and abandonment of its material cause are otherwise inexplicable, or because the cognition of the jar is otherwise inexplicable?
If it is because the purpose of the jar is otherwise inexplicable,
that is incorrect.
The jar is not the effect of cognition;
rather, in this case, cognition is the effect of that [jar].
Now, if it is argued that the postulation of cognition is made because otherwise the appropriation and abandonment of the jar would be inexplicable, [we reply:]...
That is incorrect;
since the nature of cognition cannot persist across multiple intervals of time, the *arthāpatti* (presumption) would be devoid of an object.

For someone might act toward the acquisition or avoidance of a jar either because they have been impelled by some powerful force without the mediation of cognition, or due to a derangement of that cognition; therefore, the *arthāpatti* is of doubtful validity.
Furthermore, without the apprehension of a relation, comprehension in a determinate cognition is not possible;
and since that [comprehension] would otherwise be untenable, it is difficult to even postulate the existence of the sense organ through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
Now, if the postulation of a cognition is made on the grounds that the act of understanding would otherwise be inexplicable, [then...]
Furthermore, that [cognition] also has no connection with another cognition; how then could it cause understanding?
And when understanding is apprehended, cognition is apprehended through direct perception itself, not as something accessible through [another] understanding.
Since the words *avabodha*, *buddhi*, and *vijñāna* are synonyms, they have the same meaning: "it is understood" (*avabudhyate*) and "it is known" (*jñāyate*).
Likewise, the claim that the functioning of the ear and other senses is non-conceptual has also been refuted.
6.1 The transformation of the instruments, such as the ear and so forth, into the form of objects such as sound and so forth, is designated by the term "function" (*vṛtti*).
This function is of many kinds, consisting of the nature of right knowledge as well as the nature of erroneous knowledge and doubt.
As it has been said: "Tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra, and andhatāmisra," and so forth.
6.11 If, then, perceptuality belongs to the functioning of the auditory and other senses,
it follows that even the functioning of error and the like would possess perceptuality. Alternatively, the term "unsublated" (abādhita) may be introduced.
That is not heard in the Sūtra;
or even if one were to imagine it,
its non-deviation cannot be known.
And this has been explained in detail in the section on the definition of perception according to the Naiyāyikas.

Furthermore, if the term "non-erroneous" (avyabhicārin) were used to exclude only the cognitive state consisting of error (viparyaya), then the correct state of cognition (samyag-rūpā vṛttiḥ), which is established as being of that same nature [as the erroneous one], would also be excluded.
Consequently, no mode of existence (*vṛtti*) can be apprehended as something to be grasped.
If, on the other hand, a truly real mode of existence were to be apprehended here, then nothing could be excluded, because it is admitted that all modes of existence possess a single nature.
Or, if a difference is admitted, there is an abandonment of what has been accepted;
for according to your position, the functions do not differ from the sense organ,
and if that [organ] is non-different [from them], [the same consequence follows].

How is there a distinction between the modes of functioning (*vṛtti*)? If a distinction is admitted, the unity of the sense organ (*indriya*) is lost; or else, it must not be said that the modes are non-different from the sense organ.

6.1 If it is admitted that [the function] is non-different from the sense organ, there would be the perception of blue, red, jars, and so forth at all times, because when the sense organ is present, it is possible for its function— which is non-different from it— to be present. And if that were possible, the non-perception of jars and other such things would be untenable.
Furthermore, if there were existence through modification alone, there would never be non-perception;
nor would there ever be perception.
For in your own position, nothing new is ever produced, nor does anything previously existing ever cease.
And therefore, for everything, upon what would the perception or non-perception of existence depend?
Would it be constant perception or constant non-perception?
For one who maintains such a view, there is no second possibility.
6.1b Furthermore, regarding sound and the other [objects], are they perceived while possessing a non-perceivable nature, or are they perceived while possessing a perceivable nature?
If they are perceived while possessing a non-perceivable nature, then how can there be perception?
If they were of an unperceivable nature, how could they be perceived?
Otherwise, even the self and so forth would be perceived.
Now, if things possessing a perceivable nature are perceived,
how can there be non-perception?
Is it by that very same aspect, or rather by another aspect?
If non-apprehension occurs in that very same manner, then the non-apprehension of the self and so forth would not follow; or, if there is apprehension, another reason must be stated.
Now, if they are not perceived through another mode [of perception], even so, there is no identity between the perceived and the unperceived, as in the case of the sound-essence and its forms;
for a nature that is unperceived has never been seen to be non-different from a sound whose nature is perceived.
If, on the other hand, there is perception only of that which has been manifested,

then since manifestation exists at all times— just like the nature of the object itself— it would follow that there must be constant perception. If, however, it is argued that there is no perception when [the object] is concealed, [then...]
Because of the identity between that [non-perception] and its own nature, there would follow the consequence of constant non-perception.
Or, if both were present, perception and non-perception would occur simultaneously.
Consequently, there would be an absence of the conventional usage: "it is perceived now" and "it was not perceived previously."
Likewise, it would follow that one could not say, "I perceived it previously, but now I do not perceive it. Furthermore, if perception occurs when there is an accumulation of parts,
then because those parts exist at all times, it would follow that perception must occur at all times.
If perception occurs when there is nourishment of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*),
then because that [characteristic] exists at all times, it would follow that perception must occur constantly.
Alternatively, if perception occurs when there is excellence of configuration (*saṃsthāna*), [then...]
Since that [object] also exists at all times, there would be constant perception.
Therefore, for whatever cause one imagines the perception to arise, because that cause would exist at all times, it follows that there would be constant perception.
If non-perception occurs due to the obstruction of place, time, or causal factors (*kāraka*),

then because that obstruction would exist at all times, there would be no cessation of non-perception. Likewise, the status of the sense organs as instruments (*karaṇa*) is not perceived, due to the absence of their effects.
Is it not the case that consciousness is the fruit?
No, because it exists at all times;
for the relationship of cause and fruit is not tenable between two things that exist at all times.

Just as qualities do not stand in a causal relationship to one another, nor do distinct selves stand in such a relationship to other selves— since one self is neither the cause nor the effect of another self—
so too here, existence (*sattā*), which is without beginning or end, is said to be neither an effect nor a cause.
Furthermore, there are various effects such as earth, water, and so forth; are these distinct from the three *guṇas* or non-distinct from them?
If they were distinct, [what would follow?]
Is that [cause] real or unreal?
If it were real,
then it would not be preceded by the material cause consisting of the three qualities (guṇatraya).
Therefore, because it is distinct [from the three qualities], like the nature of the Self (*ātman*),
not even one of the other types of relations with the three qualities is possible for that which has a distinct effect from them.

There is no relation of part-to-whole (*mātrāmātrika*), nor a state of concomitance (*sahacara-sahacarita-bhāva*), nor a relation of cause-and-effect (*nimitta-naimittika-bhāva*) or benefactor-and-beneficiary (*upakārya-upakāraka-bhāva*).
Now, if it is unreal, how can the three qualities (guṇatraya) be perceived by it, given that a connection with the three qualities is logically impossible?
Furthermore, a relationship between the existent and the non-existent is not possible, just as in the case of a self and a donkey's horn.
In the absence of that [perception], there is no comprehension of the three qualities through inference;
nor is there a determination of the qualities by means of direct perception, because that itself is not admitted. As it has been said:
"The supreme form of the qualities does not come within the path of vision."
But that which has come within the range of vision is utterly void, like an illusion.
And if that [object] is not apprehended, there can be no inference of the enjoyer by means of the object of enjoyment;
consequently, neither the self nor the three qualities [would exist].
Now, if [the object] were non-different [from the subject],...
Is that [nature] real or unreal?
If it is real, then since effects are innumerable, the qualities must also be innumerable.
And therefore, one should not say "the three qualities" (trayo guṇāḥ).
If, on the other hand, there is a triad of qualities, then it follows that the effect must also be a triad.
Infinite regress would be abandoned.
Likewise, if the effect is perceptible, the qualities must also be perceptible.
Of what object, then, is the inference of the Pradhāna?

Parikh and E. Franco’s Notes:
Examination of the Inference of the Self [8.1 Refutation of the Inference of the Self as Accepted by the Naiyāyikas and Others]

Likewise, inference of the self through pleasure, aversion, cognition, and so forth is not possible, because no relationship with them is apprehended; and if that [relationship] is not apprehended, inference is purposeless.
Furthermore, what is being established here?
Is it the fact that cognition, pleasure, and so forth are dependent, or rather the nature of cognition as that which is supported by its substratum?

If, on the other hand, being dependent is what is to be proven, then it is already understood by the very nature of the self, since dependence is something other than that [self]. Or, if the self is what is to be proven...

Thus, it follows that the self exists because of consciousness; yet, there is no capacity for something residing in a different locus to serve as a probans. Alternatively, if what is being proven is the nature of consciousness itself as something dependent [on a substrate], [then the following applies].
And that [self] is apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
One must state what other object of inference (*anumāna*) there is.

How is it that cognition, pleasure, and so forth are designated as being related to the self—is it by virtue of their mere existence, or by being produced from it, or by being its producer, or by inhering in it, or by identity with its essential nature?
Or rather?
If pleasure or consciousness were attributed to the self by its mere existence, then all entities would be conscious like the self, because there is no difference in the existence of consciousness;
likewise, all would be happy, because there is no difference in the existence of bliss.
If it is argued that consciousness is designated as belonging to the self because it is produced by it,
then the eyes, light, and cloth would also be conscious, since there is no difference in their being producers [of consciousness].
If it is argued that [consciousness belongs to the self] because it is its producer, [then the same objection applies].
That is incorrect: on your view, the self is not produced by consciousness, nor is recollection possible through production.
Furthermore, if consciousness is attributed to the self because it inheres in it, that cannot be so in the absence of such a self.

Or, let it be that inherence (*samavāya*) is indeed an undivided entity common to all selves, clothes, and so forth; consequently, all things would be conscious. If you argue that what is characterized by consciousness cannot occur elsewhere, that is incorrect, because that which is characterized by it can occur elsewhere, and its occurrence there is due to its being a single entity.
Alternatively, if [inherence] does not exist, there would be the consequence of either multiple inherences or the non-inherent nature of other things.

Likewise, regarding the inherence of the self with consciousness: is it by virtue of mere existence, or by virtue of being the producer of that [consciousness], or by virtue of being produced by that, or by virtue of being inherent in that, or through identity with the very nature of the self?
If, first, inherence with the self is asserted merely by virtue of its existence;

In that case, because of the specific existence of the inherence of cognition (*jñāna-samavāya*), there would follow the undesirable consequence that all things would be substrata for the inherence of cognition.

If, on the other hand, [the status of being a substratum] were due to being produced by that [cognition], that is incorrect; for an inherence is not produced by the self, since its eternity is admitted.

Now, if it is argued that the self's inherence [in cognition] consists in its being its producer, that is untenable because the self is eternal. Or, if it is argued that it is called "inherence in the self" because it inheres in the self; [then we reply:]...

That is incorrect, because one does not admit another inherence (*samavāya*). If it is argued that "inherence in the self" is so called because it exists through identity with the self (*ātmatādātmyena*), [we reply:]...
Then, no other self exists, nor is there an inherence relation, because [the self] has entered into that very nature.
Thus, by way of an inherence relation, a designation of a fixed self for consciousness, bliss, and so forth, is not tenable.
If, however, consciousness, bliss, and so forth—which arise through identity with the self—are designated as the self, then by this line of reasoning, the self would become subject to modification.
Consequently, memory, inference, and recognition would be impossible.
For this reason as well, the self cannot be understood as the substratum of effects such as pleasure and so forth.
Is that self, which has not undergone any modification, to produce effects such as pain, or is it to do so even when a modification has been produced?
Is it by means of an excellence that has arisen as something distinct, or by means of an excellence that has arisen as something non-distinct?
If that effect, such as heat and so forth, is produced by that which has not had an excellence arise [in it], then...
Then one should always act,
because one who has not yet produced strength accepts the performance of tasks; thus, one would not be devoid of heat and so forth.
It follows that effects such as pleasure and so forth would be identical [to their cause].

Alternatively, if the effect— such as heat— is produced by means of an excellence (*atiśaya*) that has arisen without being distinct [from the cause], then what is meant by the phrase "an excellence that has arisen without being distinct"?
The self is produced;
and consequently, there would be the impossibility of memory, inference, and recognition.
Or, if the effect—such as heat and so forth—is produced by means of a newly arisen excellence distinct [from the self], [then...]
Is that [excellence] connected with that self, or not?
If it is not connected,
how can it be its excellence?
Now, if it is related, is it so by way of being a producer, or by way of being produced, or by way of being its inherent substrate?
If it is related by way of being a producer, then it is identical with itself.
Because it arises with excellence (*atiśaya*), recollection would be impossible;
or if [recollection were possible] because it is produced (*janya*), how could that [excellence] also be produced by that [same cause]?
Is it produced by that which has not acquired any excellence, or by that which has acquired a distinct excellence? Such is the resulting series of questions.
Or is it by virtue of being inherent in that [substratum]? No, because that [inherence] is common to all things.
And because of its absence [in others],
if it were connected by virtue of producing a single effect,
then this very point has begun to be considered: what indeed is this so-called "productivity"?
Furthermore, that very nature which exists when no excellence has arisen remains the same even after it has arisen; how then could it produce an effect?
Or, if its former nature were not to remain in that state, [it would follow that it is something else].
If permanence means being well-established, or if it means remaining in that same state,
even so, it does not perform any action.

Thus, according to the views of the Naiyāyikas and others, the experience, recollection, and so forth of the self do not cohere. Likewise, even according to the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, the inference of the self does not proceed, because they maintain that the objects of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be things not already determined by other means of valid cognition.

For the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operate with respect to fixed objects: inference does not function toward what is to be determined by perception, nor does perception function toward what is to be determined by inference.
Therefore, they have as their objects specific characteristics that are mutually exclusive.
That which was stated— "there is a lack of concomitance with respect to particulars"— is incorrect;
for a particular is an object grasped by a restricted means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If such an object is accepted, there would be an absence of concomitance (*anugama*) for inference;
concomitance is a relation,
and its apprehension would be impossible.
Now, even when an object has already been ascertained through perception and other means, inference still proceeds;
but if this were so, would it not follow that the object is common to both perception and inference?
"Commonality" means equality.
[The objection that] "there is the fallacy of proving what is already established regarding the universal" arises because it is apprehended through perception;
furthermore, the qualification "cognizing an object not previously cognized" is redundant.
Alternatively, the meaning is that "proof" occurs when the universal is established;
for the Mīmāṃsaka accepts a relationship of the signified and the signifier between two universals, and not that [relationship]...
The universal exists;
and how it does not exist has already been explained previously.
Consequently, this is the proving of what is already established, the proving of what already exists.
Furthermore, the nature of fire does not exist [in that which is being examined].
In its absence, of what would this be a signifier?
Alternatively, the meaning is that proving what is already established is "proving the already established" (*siddhasādhana*).
The means of proof must be existent; however, the universal "smokeness" does not exist, even though it would have to be existent [if it were the means]. (Sukhlal)
How can that [universal], which does not exist as a reality, be a universal? (Read: "that" and "in the universal")
Could it be a means of proof (*sādhana*)? Or is it that inference which is known as "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*) serves as the means of proof?
And smoke-ness (*dhūmatva*) is not itself known [as such], because it does not exist in its own right.
Alternatively, because there is no means of apprehending it, its form is interwoven;
yet that [form] is not interwoven within the self.
Nor does it reside in a single individual instance,
but rather in many individual instances; yet many individual instances are not perceived.
Rather, it is only a single individual instance of smoke that is perceived;
and there is no cognition of a universal within a single instance by way of a recurring nature,
nor is there a universal consisting of some other form.
(perhaps: another form of the universal) /
